papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a structured layerwise organization of multilingual processing in MoE LLMs and proposes a routing-guided steering method that improves multilingual performance by aligning routing behavior with dominant languages.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals a structured organization of multilingual processing in MoE LLMs across layers and languages, and demonstrates that inference-time routing steering can improve multilingual performance, particularly for linguistically related languages.
papers.key_findings:
Routing behavior aligns with linguistic families: languages within the same family share similar routing distributions.
Expert utilization shows a layerwise pattern: middle layers have higher cross-language routing similarity and fewer language-exclusive experts, acting as language-agnostic capacity hubs.
Low-resource languages rely more on language-exclusive experts but still underperform, while high-resource languages effectively use shared experts.
Interventions show that early-layer exclusive experts are crucial for language understanding, late-layer exclusive experts for maintaining language consistency, and middle-layer interventions have minimal impact.
Proposed routing-guided steering method, which biases routing in middle layers toward dominant-language experts, improves multilingual performance, with gains correlated with linguistic proximity.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is conducted on a single MoE model (Qwen3-30B-A3B); generalizability to other MoE architectures remains to be verified.
Investigation is restricted to inference-time interventions; extending to training-time optimization is future work.
future_direction: Extending insights to training-time or post-training optimization to explicitly shape expert behaviors.
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have shown strong multilingual capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms underlying performance gains and cross-language differences remain insufficiently understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic analysis of MoE models, examining routing behavior and expert specialization across languages and network depth. Our analysis reveals that multilingual processing in MoE models is highly structured: routing aligns with linguistic families, expert utilization follows a clear layerwise pattern, and high-resource languages rely on shared experts while low-resource languages depend more on language-exclusive experts despite weaker performance. Layerwise interventions further show that early and late MoE layers support language-specific processing, whereas middle layers serve as language-agnostic capacity hubs. Building on these insights, we propose a routing-guided steering method that adaptively guides routing behavior in middle layers toward shared experts associated with dominant languages at inference time, leading to consistent multilingual performance improvements, particularly for linguistically related language pairs. Our code is available at https://github.com/conctsai/Multilingualism-in-Mixture-of-Experts-LLMs.

papers.title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do disentangled representations emerge in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-task learning in evidence accumulation tasks leads to disentangled representations in the latent state of autoregressive models, with theoretical guarantees on emergence conditions.
papers.conclusion: Multi-task learning establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, explaining their generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical guarantees show that any optimal multi-task classifier must encode a maximum likelihood estimate of the ground truth in its latent state, leading to abstract and disentangled representations as the number of tasks increases.
RNNs trained on multi-task classification learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, enabling zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization.
Transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, achieving orthogonality even with fewer tasks compared to RNNs.
Noise in observations is necessary for disentangled representations to emerge, as it prevents saturation and preserves distance information.
The framework is robust to various manipulations including correlated inputs, non-linear decision boundaries, and free reaction-time tasks.
future_direction: Characterizing representation learning with multiple manifold decision boundaries
Exploring interplay between task diversity, energy constraints, and the emergence of shared representations
papers.abstract: Intelligent perception and interaction with the world hinges on internal representations that capture its underlying structure (''disentangled'' or ''abstract'' representations). Disentangled representations serve as world models, isolating latent factors of variation in the world along approximately orthogonal directions, thus facilitating feature-based generalization. We provide experimental and theoretical results guaranteeing the emergence of disentangled representations in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks, canonical in the neuroscience literature. The key conceptual finding is that, by producing accurate multi-task classification estimates, a system implicitly represents a set of coordinates specifying a disentangled representation of the underlying latent state of the data it receives. The theory provides conditions for the emergence of these representations in terms of noise, number of tasks, and evidence accumulation time. We experimentally validate these predictions in RNNs trained to multi-task, which learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, leading to zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in predicting latent factors. We demonstrate the robustness of our framework across autoregressive architectures, decision boundary geometries and in tasks requiring classification confidence estimation. We find that transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, which might explain their unique world understanding abilities. Overall, our framework establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, and helps explain why ANNs often arrive at human-interpretable concepts, and how they both may acquire exceptional zero-shot generalization capabilities.

papers.title: An effective theory of collective deep learning
papers.research_question: Does collective learning emerge when neural networks are put in interaction? Does this collective learning phase emerge abruptly, and do deep learning architectures play a non-trivial role?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a minimal model of collective learning in coupled neural networks, derives an effective theory predicting depth-dependent disorder-order-disorder phase transitions, and validates it on MNIST, showing that individual networks can generalize to unseen classes when collective learning emerges.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes a mathematical foundation for collective learning, enriching deep learning theories and statistical physics, and could contribute to tackling alignment problems in interacting learning models.
papers.key_findings:
The model exhibits disorder-order-disorder phase transitions in the parameters' solutions as coupling strength increases.
The collective learning phase emerges abruptly at a critical coupling strength, akin to a phase transition.
Deep networks show a depth-delayed onset of the collective learning phase.
The microscopic learning path is low-rank, driven by a single effective dimension (the input-output correlation vector).
Individual networks trained on private data can fully generalize to unseen data classes when the collective learning phase emerges.
papers.limitation:
The effective theory is based on simplifications and approximations, such as linear activation functions, mean square loss, one-dimensional data, and mean-field approximations.
The proof of concept does not cover the myriad of learning phases found in isolated neural networks.
future_direction: Extending the effective theory to the complex plane to capture more nuances and increase analytical tractability.
Exploring how the shape and difficulty of a dataset (encapsulated in the distribution of quenched disorders) affect the nature of phase transitions.
Investigating the effect of supra-network topology beyond the mean-field, undirected, pair-wise and time-independent case.
papers.abstract: Unraveling the emergence of collective learning in systems of coupled artificial neural networks points to broader implications for machine learning, neuroscience, and society. Here we introduce a minimal model that condenses several recent decentralized algorithms by considering a competition between two terms: the local learning dynamics in the parameters of each neural network unit, and a diffusive coupling among units that tends to homogenize the parameters of the ensemble. We derive an effective theory for linear networks to show that the coarse-grained behavior of our system is equivalent to a deformed Ginzburg-Landau model with quenched disorder. This framework predicts depth-dependent disorder-order-disorder phase transitions in the parameters' solutions that reveal a depth-delayed onset of a collective learning phase and a low-rank microscopic learning path. We validate the theory in coupled ensembles of realistic neural networks trained on the MNIST dataset under privacy constraints. Interestingly, experiments confirm that individual networks -- trained on private data -- can fully generalize to unseen data classes when the collective learning phase emerges. Our work establishes the physics of collective learning and contributes to the mechanistic interpretability of deep learning in decentralized settings.

papers.title: Towards Interpreting and Mitigating Shortcut Learning Behavior of NLU models
papers.research_question: How can shortcut learning behavior in NLU models be explained by the long-tailed phenomenon, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that shortcut learning in NLU models can be explained by a long-tailed distribution of features and introduces LTGR, a regularization method based on knowledge distillation to mitigate shortcut reliance and improve OOD generalization.
papers.conclusion: The long-tailed phenomenon explains shortcut learning in NLU models, and LTGR effectively mitigates it, improving OOD generalization while preserving in-distribution performance.
papers.key_findings:
NLU models have a strong preference for features at the head of the long-tailed distribution, which are shortcut features.
Shortcut features are picked up during very early iterations of model training.
LTGR improves generalization accuracy on out-of-distribution data while preserving accuracy on in-distribution data.
LTGR can mitigate intentionally inserted shortcut features, such as in backdoor attacks.
The Bi-LSTM classification head exacerbates shortcut learning compared to simpler heads.
papers.limitation: Models still rely to some extent on shortcut features after mitigation
future_direction: Incorporating more inductive bias or domain knowledge to further reduce shortcut reliance
papers.abstract: Mengnan Du, Varun Manjunatha, Rajiv Jain, Ruchi Deshpande, Franck Dernoncourt, Jiuxiang Gu, Tong Sun, Xia Hu. Proceedings of the 2021 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies. 2021.

papers.title: Decoding Knowledge Attribution in Mixture-of-Experts: A Framework of Basic-Refinement Collaboration and Efficiency Analysis
papers.research_question: How do experts collaboratively process and refine knowledge within MoE models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a cross-level attribution algorithm for MoE models, uncovering a 'basic-refinement' collaboration framework where shared experts handle general tasks and routed experts specialize in domain-specific processing.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a cross-level knowledge attribution algorithm for MoE models, bridging the interpretability gap between sparse and dense architectures. Uncover MoE's unique efficiency patterns and a 'basic-refinement' collaboration framework, offering actionable design guidelines.
papers.key_findings:
MoE models achieve higher per-layer efficiency via a 'mid-activation, late-amplification' pattern.
Shared experts act as generalists for foundational tasks (e.g., entity recognition) while routed experts specialize in refining domain-specific attributes (e.g., geographic reasoning).
Semantic-driven routing is evidenced by strong temporal correlations between attention heads and expert selection (r = 0.68).
Architectural depth dictates robustness: deep MoE models with shared experts mitigate expert failures through redundancy, while shallow models suffer severe degradation.
Task sensitivity guides design: core-sensitive tasks (e.g., geography) require concentrated expertise, while distributed-tolerant tasks (e.g., object attributes) leverage broader expert participation.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is confined to 7B-parameter, static-routing MoE models; it remains to be seen whether much larger (e.g., 100B+) or fully dynamic MoE architectures will exhibit the same specialization patterns.
Omits retrieval-augmented MoEs, whose external-knowledge coupling adds confounding factors beyond the scope of the study.
papers.abstract: The interpretability of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, especially those with heterogeneous designs, remains underexplored. Existing attribution methods for dense models fail to capture dynamic routing-expert interactions in sparse MoE architectures. To address this issue, we propose a cross-level attribution algorithm to analyze sparse MoE architectures (Qwen 1.5-MoE, OLMoE, Mixtral-8x7B) against dense models (Qwen 1.5-7B, Llama-7B, Mistral-7B). Results show MoE models achieve 37% higher per-layer efficiency via a "mid-activation, late-amplification" pattern: early layers screen experts, while late layers refine knowledge collaboratively. Ablation studies reveal a "basic-refinement" framework--shared experts handle general tasks (entity recognition), while routed experts specialize in domain-specific processing (geographic attributes). Semantic-driven routing is evidenced by strong correlations between attention heads and experts (r=0.68), enabling task-aware coordination. Notably, architectural depth dictates robustness: deep Qwen 1.5-MoE mitigates expert failures (e.g., 43% MRR drop in geographic tasks when blocking top-10 experts) through shared expert redundancy, whereas shallow OLMoE suffers severe degradation (76% drop). Task sensitivity further guides design: core-sensitive tasks (geography) require concentrated expertise, while distributed-tolerant tasks (object attributes) leverage broader participation. These insights advance MoE interpretability, offering principles to balance efficiency, specialization, and robustness.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Condensation of Neural Networks at Initial Training
papers.research_question: How does small initialization lead to condensation of input weights in neural networks during initial training, and how is this condensation related to the multiplicity of the activation function?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the maximal number of condensed orientations in the initial training stage is twice the multiplicity of the activation function, and provides theoretical analysis for two specific cases.
papers.conclusion: The multiplicity of the activation function is a key factor in understanding the complexity of neural network output and the weight condensation at initial training, which restricts the network to effectively low capacity initially.
papers.key_findings:
Condensation of input weights onto isolated orientations occurs during initial training with small initialization.
The maximal number of condensed orientations is twice the multiplicity p of the activation function (e.g., one line for p=1, two lines for p=2).
For common activation functions with multiplicity one (tanh, sigmoid, softplus), condensation occurs on one line (two opposite directions).
Theoretical analysis confirms the condensation bound for activation functions of multiplicity one with arbitrary input dimension, and for layers with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity.
The condensation phenomenon is observed in both synthetic data experiments and image classification tasks (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, MNIST).
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is only provided for two specific cases: activation functions of multiplicity one with arbitrary dimension input, and layers with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity. The general case with high-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity remains an open problem.
future_direction: Studying condensation for multiple-layer neural networks throughout the entire training process.
Theoretical analysis for the general case of high-dimensional input data with arbitrary multiplicity.
Investigating how training data (e.g., frequency, complexity) affects the condensation phenomenon.
papers.abstract: Empirical works show that for ReLU neural networks (NNs) with small initialization, input weights of hidden neurons (the input weight of a hidden neuron consists of the weight from its input layer to the hidden neuron and its bias term) condense on isolated orientations. The condensation dynamics implies that the training implicitly regularizes a NN towards one with a much smaller effective size. In this work, we illustrate the formation of the condensation in multi-layer fully connected NNs and show that the maximal number of condensed orientations in the initial training stage is twice the multiplicity of the activation function, where "multiplicity" indicates the multiple roots of activation function at origin. Our theoretical analysis confirms experiments for two cases, one is for the activation function of multiplicity one with arbitrary dimension input, which contains many common activation functions, and the other is for the layer with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity. This work makes a step towards understanding how small initialization leads NNs to condensation at the initial training stage.

papers.title: Mixture of Cognitive Reasoners: Modular Reasoning with Brain-Like Specialization
papers.research_question: How can we design a modular language model that exhibits brain-like functional specialization to improve interpretability, controllability, and alignment with human behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mixture of Cognitive Reasoners (MICRO), a brain-inspired modular language model that induces interpretable functional specialization, enables dynamic steering via token routing, and achieves competitive performance with improved human behavioral alignment.
papers.conclusion: Cognitively grounded functional specialization yields models that are both more human-like and more human-interpretable.
papers.key_findings:
The experts become specialized and interpretable: routing patterns show domain-specific specialization (e.g., logic expert for math tasks).
Ablating an expert causes performance drops on tasks requiring its domain, showing causal meaningfulness.
Neuroscience localizers can recover the corresponding experts in the model, supporting brain-like specialization.
MICRO models show stronger alignment to human behavior on COGBENCH compared to baselines.
MICRO achieves competitive performance on reasoning benchmarks while maintaining interpretability.
papers.limitation:
ToM localization is less effective at isolating units within the social experts, possibly due to limited stimulus set size.
MoE architecture does not reliably induce specialization in models larger than 1.5B parameters.
papers.abstract: Human cognitive behavior arises from the interaction of specialized brain networks dedicated to distinct functions, such as language, logic, and social reasoning. Inspired by this organization, we propose Mixture of Cognitive Reasoners (MiCRo): a modular, transformer-based architecture post-trained with a curriculum that induces functional specialization across experts. Concretely, we partition the layers of a pretrained language model into four expert modules aligned with well-studied cognitive networks in the human brain. MiCRo offers three key advantages over standard language models. (1) The specialized experts are interpretable and causally meaningful -- ablating a module causes substantial drops on benchmarks requiring its specialized domain. (2) MiCRo's behavior can be dynamically steered at inference time by routing tokens to particular experts (e.g., favoring social over logical reasoning), enabling fine-grained control over outputs. (3) MiCRo outperforms or matches comparable baselines on both machine-learning reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, BBH) and alignment to human behavior (CogBench), while maintaining interpretability. Taken together, cognitively grounded functional specialization yields models that are both more human-like and more human-interpretable.

papers.title: Mixture of Experts Made Intrinsically Interpretable
papers.research_question: How can we design Mixture-of-Experts models to be intrinsically interpretable by making them wide and sparse, and what architectural choices enhance interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: We introduce MoE-X, a Mixture-of-Experts model designed to be intrinsically interpretable by making it wide and sparse, using ReLU experts and sparsity-aware routing, achieving competitive performance and improved interpretability.
papers.conclusion: MoE-X demonstrates that Mixture-of-Experts models can be designed to be intrinsically interpretable by enforcing sparsity and using sparsity-aware routing, achieving both high performance and transparent internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Wider and sparser networks lead to more interpretable neurons.
MoE models naturally align with wide and sparse architectures, making them suitable for intrinsic interpretability.
MoE-X outperforms dense models and other MoE variants in interpretability while maintaining competitive performance.
MoE-X beats sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches in interpretability with greater faithfulness.
Sparsity-aware routing effectively selects experts with the sparsest activations, enhancing interpretability.
papers.limitation: Identifying the optimal sparsity level for interpretability remains difficult.
papers.abstract: Neurons in large language models often exhibit \emph{polysemanticity}, simultaneously encoding multiple unrelated concepts and obscuring interpretability. Instead of relying on post-hoc methods, we present \textbf{MoE-X}, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model designed to be \emph{intrinsically} interpretable. Our approach is motivated by the observation that, in language models, wider networks with sparse activations are more likely to capture interpretable factors. However, directly training such large sparse networks is computationally prohibitive. MoE architectures offer a scalable alternative by activating only a subset of experts for any given input, inherently aligning with interpretability objectives. In MoE-X, we establish this connection by rewriting the MoE layer as an equivalent sparse, large MLP. This approach enables efficient scaling of the hidden size while maintaining sparsity. To further enhance interpretability, we enforce sparse activation within each expert and redesign the routing mechanism to prioritize experts with the highest activation sparsity. These designs ensure that only the most salient features are routed and processed by the experts. We evaluate MoE-X on chess and natural language tasks, showing that it achieves performance comparable to dense models while significantly improving interpretability. MoE-X achieves a perplexity better than GPT-2, with interpretability surpassing even sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based approaches.

papers.title: Pathologies of Neural Models Make Interpretations Difficult
papers.research_question: Why do existing feature attribution interpretation methods for neural models fail, and how can the pathological behaviors they expose (e.g., overconfidence on nonsensical inputs) be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces input reduction, a method that exposes pathological behaviors in neural models (overconfidence on nonsensical, reduced inputs) and shows that fine-tuning with entropy regularization on these reduced examples mitigates the pathologies without harming accuracy on regular examples.
papers.conclusion: Input reduction reveals fundamental difficulties in interpreting neural models due to overconfidence and sensitivity, and suggests that improving uncertainty estimation and moving beyond bag-of-word heatmaps are important future directions for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Input reduction can iteratively remove 'unimportant' words from an input, often reducing it to one or two nonsensical words, without changing the model's prediction or significantly lowering its confidence.
Neural models are overconfident on these reduced 'rubbish' examples, which humans cannot answer correctly, revealing a failure of uncertainty estimation.
Gradient-based interpretation methods exhibit second-order sensitivity, where small input changes cause large shifts in the interpretation heatmap, even when the prediction remains stable.
Fine-tuning models with entropy regularization on reduced examples increases the length and human-interpretability of the reduced inputs without sacrificing accuracy on regular examples.
The pathologies are not due to overfitting alone, as they appear early in training, and are a fundamental issue with maximum likelihood training objectives.
future_direction: more thorough evaluation of interpretation methods
better uncertainty and confidence estimates
interpretation beyond bag-of-word heatmap
papers.abstract: One way to interpret neural model predictions is to highlight the most important input features-for example, a heatmap visualization over the words in an input sentence. In existing interpretation methods for NLP, a word's importance is determined by either input perturbation-measuring the decrease in model confidence when that word is removed-or by the gradient with respect to that word. To understand the limitations of these methods, we use input reduction, which iteratively removes the least important word from the input. This exposes pathological behaviors of neural models: the remaining words appear nonsensical to humans and are not the ones determined as important by interpretation methods. As we confirm with human experiments, the reduced examples lack information to support the prediction of any label, but models still make the same predictions with high confidence. To explain these counterintuitive results, we draw connections to adversarial examples and confidence calibration: pathological behaviors reveal difficulties in interpreting neural models trained with maximum likelihood. To mitigate their deficiencies, we fine-tune the models by encouraging high entropy outputs on reduced examples. Fine-tuned models become more interpretable under input reduction without accuracy loss on regular examples.

papers.title: A framework for the emergence and analysis of language in social learning agents
papers.research_question: How are internal representations structured and optimized for communication between agents in social learning, and how does language emerge from such interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework with a sparse autoencoder to study emergent communication, showing that student feedback shapes the language embedding to prioritize policy information, improving task performance and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides insights into how language emerges from social interactions and how communication constraints shape internal representations, with implications for generalization in cooperative multi-agent systems.
papers.key_findings:
Providing teacher information to the student leads to higher task completion rates and the ability to generalize to unseen tasks.
Optimizing message content with student feedback improves information encoding, altering the latent structure to focus on policy (goal location and initial action) rather than state space (wall position).
The emergent communication exhibits properties of natural language such as compositionality (topographic similarity) and pressure towards entropy minimization.
Feeding back the student's own task information (closing-the-loop) retains some task-relevant information but results in degraded performance and loss of generalization to unknown goals.
Bi-directional communication (with feedback) is critical for transmitting helpful information and enhances the reconstruction capability of the autoencoder.
future_direction: Understanding how social agents reconcile abstractions from their own experience with those acquired through communication.
Achieving a balance between tutoring and learning in multi-task and multi-agent systems to maintain a relevant and generalizable message space.
papers.abstract: Neural systems have evolved not only to solve environmental challenges through internal representations but also, under social constraints, to communicate these to conspecifics. In this work, we aim to understand the structure of these internal representations and how they may be optimized to transmit pertinent information from one individual to another. Thus, we build on previous teacher-student communication protocols to analyze the formation of individual and shared abstractions and their impact on task performance. We use reinforcement learning in grid-world mazes where a teacher network passes a message to a student to improve task performance. This framework allows us to relate environmental variables with individual and shared representations. We compress high-dimensional task information within a low-dimensional representational space to mimic natural language features. In coherence with previous results, we find that providing teacher information to the student leads to a higher task completion rate and an ability to generalize tasks it has not seen before. Further, optimizing message content to maximize student reward improves information encoding, suggesting that an accurate representation in the space of messages requires bi-directional input. These results highlight the role of language as a common representation among agents and its implications on generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Hidden Breakthroughs in Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How can we identify hidden breakthroughs in language model training that are obscured by the aggregate loss curve?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces POLCA, a method to decompose loss changes along basis vectors to identify hidden breakthroughs and skill acquisition during model training.
papers.conclusion: POLCA clustering identifies learned skills from decomposed loss trajectories and supports the hypothesis that high-dimensional learning involves a series of breakthroughs at various scales.
papers.key_findings:
POLCA can identify hidden breakthroughs in training that are not visible in the aggregate loss curve.
In arithmetic addition, POLCA clustering recovers the carry skill, which is not recoverable from exact loss curves.
In language modeling, POLCA clustering reveals clusters corresponding to grammatical constructions like appositive noun phrases.
The method demonstrates that models undergo multiple breakthroughs at different scales during training.
POLCA provides a tool for unsupervised interpretability by identifying skill acquisition events.
papers.limitation: The trained models may contain biases from the training datasets.
papers.abstract: Loss curves are smooth during most of model training, so visible discontinuities stand out as possible conceptual breakthroughs. Studying these breakthroughs enables a deeper understanding of learning dynamics, but only when they are properly identified. This paper argues that similar breakthroughs occur frequently throughout training but they are obscured by a loss metric that collapses all variation into a single scalar. To find these hidden transitions, we introduce POLCA, a method for decomposing changes in loss along arbitrary bases of the low-rank training subspace. We use our method to identify clusters of samples that share similar changes in loss during training, disaggregating the overall loss into that of smaller groups of conceptually similar data. We validate our method on synthetic arithmetic and natural language tasks, showing that POLCA recovers clusters that represent interpretable breakthroughs in the model's capabilities. We demonstrate the promise of these hidden phase transitions as a tool for unsupervised interpretability.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Are Neural Nets Modular? Inspecting Functional Modularity Through\n Differentiable Weight Masks
papers.research_question: Does functional modularity emerge in neural networks, and to what extent do they enable compositionality?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method based on differentiable binary weight masks to identify functional modules in pre-trained neural networks, and uses it to show that typical NNs exhibit specialization but not reuse, failing to learn compositional solutions.
papers.conclusion: Standard neural networks do not naturally learn functional modularity that enables compositionality, and data routing is a key challenge that calls for new inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Typical neural networks exhibit specialization (Pspecialize) but not reuse (Preuse).
Weight sharing is driven more by shared input/output locations than by task similarity.
Neural networks fail to learn compositional solutions, as evidenced by poor systematic generalization on SCAN and the Mathematics Dataset.
In CNNs, subsets of weights responsible for single classes can be identified, and removing them causes significant performance drop on that class.
The method of differentiable weight masks can stably identify functional modules across various architectures.
papers.limitation:
The mask inversion method is limited to analyzing entirely disjoint weights.
The straight-through estimator used in mask training introduces approximations in gradient calculations.
future_direction: Research on suitable inductive biases for data routing and modularity in neural networks.
Further investigation into how to incorporate biases that separate data transformation and information routing.
papers.abstract:
Neural networks (NNs) whose subnetworks implement reusable functions are
expected to offer numerous advantages, including compositionality through
efficient recombination of functional building blocks, interpretability,
preventing catastrophic interference, etc. Understanding if and how NNs are
modular could provide insights into how to improve them. Current inspection
methods, however, fail to link modules to their functionality. In this paper,
we present a novel method based on learning binary weight masks to identify
individual weights and subnets responsible for specific functions. Using this
powerful tool, we contribute an extensive study of emerging modularity in NNs
that covers several standard architectures and datasets. We demonstrate how
common NNs fail to reuse submodules and offer new insights into the related
issue of systematic generalization on language tasks.

papers.title: MLLM Machine Unlearning via Visual Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How can we effectively unlearn visual knowledge in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving textual knowledge, and how robust is this unlearning against relearning attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel MLLM unlearning approach that uses Visual Knowledge Distillation (VKD) to erase target visual knowledge while preserving textual knowledge, and is efficient by only fine-tuning the visual module.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MLLM unlearning approach effectively forgets target visual knowledge while preserving textual knowledge and is robust against relearning attacks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed VKD method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both unlearning effectiveness and model utility.
The VKD module facilitates forgetting of target visual knowledge and helps preserve visual knowledge of non-target entities.
The method is efficient due to partial fine-tuning of only the visual module.
The approach is robust against relearning attacks, as forgotten visual knowledge is not easily recovered.
The method effectively disentangles textual knowledge from visual knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recently, machine unlearning approaches have been proposed to remove sensitive information from well-trained large models. However, most existing methods are tailored for LLMs, while MLLM-oriented unlearning remains at its early stage. Inspired by recent studies exploring the internal mechanisms of MLLMs, we propose to disentangle the visual and textual knowledge embedded within MLLMs and introduce a dedicated approach to selectively erase target visual knowledge while preserving textual knowledge. Unlike previous unlearning methods that rely on output-level supervision, our approach introduces a Visual Knowledge Distillation (VKD) scheme, which leverages intermediate visual representations within the MLLM as supervision signals. This design substantially enhances both unlearning effectiveness and model utility. Moreover, since our method only fine-tunes the visual components of the MLLM, it offers significant efficiency advantages. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art unlearning methods in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency. Moreover, we are the first to evaluate the robustness of MLLM unlearning against relearning attacks.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning Chains through Depth-Specialized Mixture-of-Experts in Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be made more efficient by adapting computational depth to input complexity using a mixture of depth-specialized experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DS-MoE, a transformer-based framework that dynamically allocates computational depth by composing specialized expert modules into reasoning chains, improving efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DS-MoE demonstrates that depth-adaptive expert selection can simultaneously improve efficiency, reasoning quality, and interpretability in large-scale language models.
papers.key_findings:
DS-MoE achieves up to 70% computational savings and 2x faster inference compared to uniform-depth transformers.
DS-MoE delivers higher accuracy (up to 5.3% improvement) on complex reasoning tasks like legal and long-context datasets.
The architecture reduces GPU memory footprint by 35-40% compared to baseline models.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of routing, memory integration experts, and meta-cognitive experts for performance.
DS-MoE generates more interpretable reasoning chains, offering transparency into the decision process.
papers.limitation:
The routing network introduces overhead that may impact latency, especially in real-time settings.
Effectiveness depends on the availability of suitably specialized expert modules, which may require domain-specific development and limit generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating reinforcement learning for routing optimization.
Introducing domain-specific experts.
Generalizing DS-MoE to multimodal reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Contemporary transformer architectures apply identical processing depth to all inputs, creating inefficiencies and limiting reasoning quality. Simple factual queries are subjected to the same multilayered computation as complex logical problems, wasting resources while constraining deep inference. To overcome this, we came up with a concept of Dynamic Reasoning Chains through Depth Specialised Mixture of Experts (DS-MoE), a modular framework that extends the Mixture of Experts paradigm from width-based to depth specialised computation. DS-MoE introduces expert modules optimised for distinct reasoning depths, shallow pattern recognition, compositional reasoning, logical inference, memory integration, and meta-cognitive supervision. A learned routing network dynamically assembles custom reasoning chains, activating only the necessary experts to match input complexity. The dataset on which we trained and evaluated DS-MoE is on The Pile, an 800GB corpus covering diverse domains such as scientific papers, legal texts, programming code, and web content, enabling systematic assessment across reasoning depths. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-MoE achieves up to 16 per cent computational savings and 35 per cent faster inference compared to uniform-depth transformers, while delivering 2.8 per cent higher accuracy on complex multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, routing decisions yield interpretable reasoning chains, enhancing transparency and scalability. These findings establish DS-MoE as a significant advancement in adaptive neural architectures, demonstrating that depth-specialised modular processing can simultaneously improve efficiency, reasoning quality, and interpretability in large-scale language models.

papers.title: Universal Properties of Activation Sparsity in Modern Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the universal properties of activation sparsity across diverse Large Language Model families and scales, and how does sparsity robustness vary with model size, training strategies, and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a general framework for evaluating activation sparsity robustness in LLMs, discovers that critical sparsity increases with model size, and presents the first study of activation sparsity in diffusion-based LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation sparsity is a universal property in modern LLMs with increasing relevance at scale, offering practical opportunities for efficiency gains and providing guidelines for future sparsity-aware model design.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate activations exhibit the highest tolerance to sparsity among FFN components.
Critical sparsity (the highest sparsity with ≤1% performance drop) tends to increase with model size across families.
Instruction-tuned models generally show greater tolerance to activation sparsity than their pretrained counterparts.
Activation sparsity patterns and robustness vary significantly across different downstream tasks.
In Mixture-of-Experts models, sparsity levels are consistent across experts within a layer, with low inter-expert variance.
papers.abstract: Activation sparsity is an intriguing property of deep neural networks that has been extensively studied in ReLU-based models, due to its advantages for efficiency, robustness, and interpretability. However, methods relying on exact zero activations do not directly apply to modern Large Language Models (LLMs), leading to fragmented, model-specific strategies for LLM activation sparsity and a gap in its general understanding. In this work, we introduce a general framework for evaluating sparsity robustness in contemporary LLMs and conduct a systematic investigation of this phenomenon in their feedforward~(FFN) layers. Our results uncover universal properties of activation sparsity across diverse model families and scales. Importantly, we observe that the potential for effective activation sparsity grows with model size, highlighting its increasing relevance as models scale. Furthermore, we present the first study of activation sparsity in diffusion-based LLMs. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive perspective and practical guidance for harnessing activation sparsity in LLM design and acceleration.

papers.title: Understanding Distributed Representations of Concepts in Deep Neural Networks without Supervision
papers.research_question: How can we understand the distributed representations of concepts in deep neural networks without supervision by selecting a principal subset of neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an unsupervised method for discovering distributed representations of concepts in deep neural networks by selecting a principal subset of neurons and constructing Relaxed Decision Regions (RDRs) using a novel Configuration distance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a way to understand learned concepts in DNNs without human supervision, and it can be used for various applications like subclass detection and misclassification reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Configuration distance effectively captures instances with similar concepts compared to Euclidean and Cosine distances.
The RDR framework can identify coherent concepts, including unlabeled subclasses, without human supervision.
The method can reason about misclassifications by identifying spurious correlations encoded in internal neurons.
The method reveals layer-wise differences in concept representations: lower layers capture spatial information, while higher layers capture class-specific features.
The method outperforms existing methods (KNN, CAR, CAV, RI) in terms of purity and entropy for subclass grouping on the Oxford-pet dataset.
papers.abstract: Understanding intermediate representations of the concepts learned by deep learning classifiers is indispensable for interpreting general model behaviors. Existing approaches to reveal learned concepts often rely on human supervision, such as pre-defined concept sets or segmentation processes. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised method for discovering distributed representations of concepts by selecting a principal subset of neurons. Our empirical findings demonstrate that instances with similar neuron activation states tend to share coherent concepts. Based on the observations, the proposed method selects principal neurons that construct an interpretable region, namely a Relaxed Decision Region (RDR), encompassing instances with coherent concepts in the feature space. It can be utilized to identify unlabeled subclasses within data and to detect the causes of misclassifications. Furthermore, the applicability of our method across various layers discloses distinct distributed representations over the layers, which provides deeper insights into the internal mechanisms of the deep learning model.

papers.title: Facts as Experts: Adaptable and Interpretable Neural Memory over Symbolic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we interface a neural language model with an interpretable symbolic memory to make knowledge accessible and modifiable without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural language model (Facts-as-Experts) with an explicit interface to a symbolic fact memory, enabling knowledge updates without retraining and improving performance on knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method for interfacing a neural language model with a symbolic memory, demonstrating improved QA performance and the ability to modify knowledge without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
FaE outperforms baseline models (FOFE, EmQL, EaE) on FreebaseQA and WebQuestionsSP QA datasets.
FaE can effectively answer questions using new facts injected into its memory at inference time without retraining.
FaE can update stale memories by overwriting facts, though performance decreases when new facts contradict pretraining data.
Removing overlapping entity pairs between pretraining/finetuning and test data reduces performance, indicating some memorization of paraphrases.
FaE shows a zero-shot capability, answering around a quarter of answerable questions without fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: Updating stale memories (where new facts contradict pretraining data) is more difficult and results in a performance drop, indicating the mixing between contextual representations and knowledge requires further research.
future_direction: Addressing the difficulty of updating stale memories and the problem of deleting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Massive language models are the core of modern NLP modeling and have been shown to encode impressive amounts of commonsense and factual information. However, that knowledge exists only within the latent parameters of the model, inaccessible to inspection and interpretation, and even worse, factual information memorized from the training corpora is likely to become stale as the world changes. Knowledge stored as parameters will also inevitably exhibit all of the biases inherent in the source materials. To address these problems, we develop a neural language model that includes an explicit interface between symbolically interpretable factual information and subsymbolic neural knowledge. We show that this model dramatically improves performance on two knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks. More interestingly, the model can be updated without re-training by manipulating its symbolic representations. In particular this model allows us to add new facts and overwrite existing ones in ways that are not possible for earlier models.

papers.title: A Note on Normalized Emergence Timing (in Pythia Language Model Evaluations)
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Pythia, a suite of 16 LLMs trained on public data in the same order with 154 checkpoints each, and provides tools to reconstruct exact training dataloaders, enabling controlled studies on training dynamics and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The highly controlled setup of the Pythia suite can yield novel insights into LLMs and their training dynamics, facilitating future research.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias can be reduced by swapping pronouns in the last portion of training, with larger models showing greater reduction.
Memorization follows a Poisson point process and is not influenced by the location of a sequence in the training data.
The impact of pretraining term frequencies on few-shot performance emerges after a phase change at 65,000 steps for models with 2.8B parameters or more.
papers.limitation: The noisiness in the progression of gender bias metrics may reflect actual changes or poor reliability of the CrowS-Pairs benchmark.
future_direction: Further study of interventions (modifying training data) for bias mitigation and other applications.
Investigation of the reliability of the CrowS-Pairs benchmark.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale? To answer these questions, we introduce \textit{Pythia}, a suite of 16 LLMs all trained on public data seen in the exact same order and ranging in size from 70M to 12B parameters. We provide public access to 154 checkpoints for each one of the 16 models, alongside tools to download and reconstruct their exact training dataloaders for further study. We intend \textit{Pythia} to facilitate research in many areas, and we present several case studies including novel results in memorization, term frequency effects on few-shot performance, and reducing gender bias. We demonstrate that this highly controlled setup can be used to yield novel insights toward LLMs and their training dynamics. Trained models, analysis code, training code, and training data can be found at \url{https://github.com/EleutherAI/pythia}.

papers.title: On Semantic Cognition, Inductive Generalization, and Language Models
papers.research_question: What kinds of inductive generalizations about concepts are made by language models? To what extent do language models recognize and use emergent features during induction? How do the inductive generalization capacities of language models relate to their representational space?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an inductive reasoning-based framework to analyze semantic cognition and generalization in language models, drawing insights from cognitive science.
future_direction: Investigate inductive generalizations in language models
Study recognition and use of emergent features during induction
Analyze relationship between inductive generalization and representational space
papers.abstract: My doctoral research focuses on understanding semantic knowledge in neural network models trained solely to predict natural language (referred to as language models, or LMs), by drawing on insights from the study of concepts and categories grounded in cognitive science. I propose a framework inspired by 'inductive reasoning,' a phenomenon that sheds light on how humans utilize background knowledge to make inductive leaps and generalize from new pieces of information about concepts and their properties. Drawing from experiments that study inductive reasoning, I propose to analyze semantic inductive generalization in LMs using phenomena observed in human-induction literature, investigate inductive behavior on tasks such as implicit reasoning and emergent feature recognition, and analyze and relate induction dynamics to the learned conceptual representation space.

papers.title: Unveiling Instruction-Specific Neurons & Experts: An Analytical Framework for LLM's Instruction-Following Capabilities
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning reconfigure the internal computational mechanisms of LLMs to achieve superior instruction following?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SPARCOM framework to identify and analyze instruction-specific neurons and experts, revealing how fine-tuning shapes LLMs through sparse computational components.
papers.conclusion: This study provides novel insights into how instruction tuning shapes LLMs through sparse components, demonstrating how targeted modifications to these components significantly enhance instruction-following capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Identified instruction-specific neurons (ISNs) and experts (ISEs) that are crucial for processing and executing instructions.
ISNs and ISEs exhibit both generality (overlap across instruction types) and uniqueness (high similarity within the same instruction type).
The fundamental layer-wise distribution pattern of ISNs remains largely unchanged after fine-tuning, but the number of specialized ISNs increases.
Fine-tuning significantly alters the activation patterns of ISNs for the same instruction, while the activation of experts remains highly correlated.
Proposes a three-phase mechanistic framework (early, intermediate, final) to explain the operational principles of ISNs in both dense and MoE models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not develop strategies to leverage the identified instruction-specific components to enhance the model's instruction-following capabilities and task-solving performance.
The analysis is limited to six representative instruction types, which may not capture the full diversity of instructions.
future_direction: Explore larger and more diverse datasets to identify a broader range of Instruction-Specific Neurons and Experts, enhancing the generalizability of the findings.
papers.abstract: The finetuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced their instruction-following capabilities, yet the underlying computational mechanisms driving these improvements remain poorly understood. This study systematically examines how fine-tuning reconfigures LLM computations by isolating and analyzing instruction-specific sparse components, i.e., neurons in dense models and both neurons and experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. In particular, we introduce HexaInst, a carefully curated and balanced instructional dataset spanning six distinct categories, and propose SPARCOM, a novel analytical framework comprising three key contributions: (1) a method for identifying these sparse components, (2) an evaluation of their functional generality and uniqueness, and (3) a systematic comparison of their alterations. Through experiments, we demonstrate functional generality, uniqueness, and the critical role of these components in instruction execution. By elucidating the relationship between fine-tuning-induced adaptations and sparse computational substrates, this work provides deeper insights into how LLMs internalize instruction-following behavior for the trustworthy LLM community.

papers.title: Understanding the Behaviors of BERT in Ranking
papers.research_question: What are the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks on MS MARCO and TREC Web Track?
papers.core_contribution: BERT is effective for QA-focused passage ranking due to its interaction-based seq2seq matching, but less effective for ad hoc document ranking where user click signals are more beneficial.
papers.conclusion: BERT excels in seq2seq matching tasks like MS MARCO due to its pre-training on surrounding contexts, but for ad hoc document ranking, pre-training on user clicks is more effective.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-based rankers outperform previous neural IR models on MS MARCO passage ranking.
BERT is not effective as a representation-based model for ranking; it relies on cross-sequence interactions.
On TREC ad hoc ranking, BERT underperforms compared to feature-based learning to rank and models pre-trained on user clicks.
BERT's attention focuses on marker tokens and stopwords, but stopwords have minimal impact on performance.
BERT assigns extreme ranking scores and depends on a few key terms, preferring semantic matches over loose relevance.
papers.limitation: BERT performs worse on TREC ad hoc ranking compared to models pre-trained on user clicks, indicating a gap between its pre-training on surrounding contexts and the needs of document ranking.
future_direction: Training deeper networks on user clicks signals
Studying deeper models trained on relevance-based labels compared to shallower neural rankers
papers.abstract: This paper studies the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks. We explore several different ways to leverage the pre-trained BERT and fine-tune it on two ranking tasks: MS MARCO passage reranking and TREC Web Track ad hoc document ranking. Experimental results on MS MARCO demonstrate the strong effectiveness of BERT in question-answering focused passage ranking tasks, as well as the fact that BERT is a strong interaction-based seq2seq matching model. Experimental results on TREC show the gaps between the BERT pre-trained on surrounding contexts and the needs of ad hoc document ranking. Analyses illustrate how BERT allocates its attentions between query-document tokens in its Transformer layers, how it prefers semantic matches between paraphrase tokens, and how that differs with the soft match patterns learned by a click-trained neural ranker.

papers.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the hidden states in models of different scales? The paper investigates whether there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models trained on similar data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Linear Representation Transferability (LRT) Hypothesis and provides empirical evidence that affine mappings between hidden states of different-sized models can transfer steering vectors, enabling small models to steer large models.
papers.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence for the LRT hypothesis, suggesting that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the hypothesis is a promising direction for understanding representation alignment across model scales.
papers.key_findings:
Affine mappings can be learned between the hidden states of small and large models from the same family.
Steering vectors learned on small models retain their semantic effect when transferred to large models via the learned affine map.
The transferred steering vectors are as effective as those learned directly on the large model for tasks like refusal behavior removal and logit-based evaluation.
The feature spaces of models, as represented by sparse autoencoder decoder matrices, are approximately linearly related.
The conceptual framework of a universal representation space provides a plausible explanation for the linear transferability.
papers.limitation:
The limits of transferability across very different model sizes (e.g., 100M to 70B) are not yet understood.
Transferability across different model families or architectures is challenging due to differences in tokenization schemes and architectural design.
future_direction: Investigating the limits of transferability across model sizes.
Exploring transferability across different model families and architectures.
Developing theoretical foundations for the LRT hypothesis and the universal representation space.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that neural networks with similar architectures trained on similar data learn shared representations relevant to the learning task. We build on this idea by extending the conceptual framework where representations learned across models trained on the same data can be expressed as linear combinations of a \emph{universal} set of basis features. These basis features underlie the learning task itself and remain consistent across models, regardless of scale. From this framework, we propose the \textbf{Linear Representation Transferability (LRT)} Hypothesis -- that there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models. To test this hypothesis, we learn affine mappings between the hidden states of models of different sizes and evaluate whether steering vectors -- directions in hidden state space associated with specific model behaviors -- retain their semantic effect when transferred from small to large language models using the learned mappings. We find strong empirical evidence that such affine mappings can preserve steering behaviors. These findings suggest that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the LRT hypothesis may be a promising direction on understanding representation alignment across model scales.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: Interpreting Pretrained Contextualized Representations via Reductions to Static Embeddings
papers.research_question: Can we convert pretrained contextualized representations to static embeddings to leverage mature static embedding interpretability methods, and what do we learn about representational quality and social bias through this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces simple, general methods for converting contextualized representations to static embeddings, enabling the use of static embedding interpretability methods. Analysis reveals that pooling over many contexts improves representational quality and that social bias is encoded disparately across models and layers.
papers.conclusion: Converting contextualized representations to static embeddings is a viable approach for interpretability, revealing important insights about representational quality and bias, and enabling the use of mature static embedding analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Pooling over many contexts (aggregated strategy) significantly improves the representational quality of static embeddings derived from contextualized models.
The best-performing layer for static embeddings shifts to later layers as the number of contexts increases.
Static embeddings derived from contextualized models can outperform traditional static embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe on word similarity tasks.
Social bias is encoded disparately across different pretrained models and across different layers of the same model.
Existing bias estimators for word embeddings are dramatically inconsistent with each other.
papers.limitation:
The study only addresses a restricted subset of social biases and does not cover intersectional biases.
Existing bias estimators are inconsistent and may not reliably estimate bias.
future_direction: Investigate how the reduction to static embeddings affects different models and what it reflects about linguistic knowledge.
papers.abstract: Contextualized representations (e.g. ELMo, BERT) have become the default pretrained representations for downstream NLP applications. In some settings, this transition has rendered their static embedding predecessors (e.g. Word2Vec, GloVe) obsolete. As a side-effect, we observe that older interpretability methods for static embeddings -while more mature than those available for their dynamic counterparts -are underutilized in studying newer contextualized representations. Consequently, we introduce simple and fully general methods for converting from contextualized representations to static lookup-table embeddings which we apply to 5 popular pretrained models and 9 sets of pretrained weights. Our analysis of the resulting static embeddings notably reveals that pooling over many contexts significantly improves representational quality under intrinsic evaluation. Complementary to analyzing representational quality, we consider social biases encoded in pretrained representations with respect to gender, race/ethnicity, and religion and find that bias is encoded disparately across pretrained models and internal layers even for models that share the same training data. Concerningly, we find dramatic inconsistencies between social bias estimators for word embeddings.

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.

papers.title: Understanding and Leveraging the Expert Specialization of Context Faithfulness in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.research_question: Do context-faithful experts exist within MoE models, and how can they be leveraged for improved context faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Router Lens to identify context-faithful experts in MoE models and introduces CEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that matches or surpasses full fine-tuning.
