Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What is the origin of generalization in grokking? Why does the training time needed to generalize diverge as training set size decreases? Under what conditions does delayed generalization occur?
papers.core_contribution: Provides an effective theory and phase diagrams to explain grokking, showing that generalization arises from structured representations and that grokking can be understood as a phase between comprehension and memorization.
papers.conclusion: This study provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking and highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, such as effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Generalization in grokking originates from structured representations, whose dynamics are predicted by an effective theory.
There are four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion, with representation learning occurring only in a 'Goldilocks zone'.
On transformers, the grokking phase stays closer to memorization, leading to delayed generalization.
The critical training set size corresponds to the least amount of data needed to determine a good representation.
Grokking can be remedied with proper hyperparameter tuning, as shown in phase diagrams.
papers.limitation: The effective theory is based on Euclidean distance between embeddings and might not capture other metrics defined by the decoder.
future_direction: Generalizing the effective theory to use metrics beyond Euclidean distance.
Investigating modifications to the effective theory to account for repulsion among different classes in image classification.
papers.abstract: We aim to understand grokking, a phenomenon where models generalize long after overfitting their training set. We present both a microscopic analysis anchored by an effective theory and a macroscopic analysis of phase diagrams describing learning performance across hyperparameters. We find that generalization originates from structured representations whose training dynamics and dependence on training set size can be predicted by our effective theory in a toy setting. We observe empirically the presence of four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion. We find representation learning to occur only in a "Goldilocks zone" (including comprehension and grokking) between memorization and confusion. We find on transformers the grokking phase stays closer to the memorization phase (compared to the comprehension phase), leading to delayed generalization. The Goldilocks phase is reminiscent of "intelligence from starvation" in Darwinian evolution, where resource limitations drive discovery of more efficient solutions. This study not only provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking, but also highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, e.g., effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: Synergistic information supports modality integration and flexible learning in neural networks solving multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How does synergistic information emerge in neural networks and how does it support modality integration and flexible learning in multiple tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Synergistic information increases as networks learn multiple diverse tasks and is crucial for tasks requiring integration of multiple sources, supporting modality integration and flexible learning.
papers.conclusion: Synergistic information processing is linked to the ability to perform multiple complex tasks requiring flexibility and integration, aligning with findings in neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout increases redundancy in hidden layers and removes irrelevant input information.
Performance relies on synergistic neurons, especially for tasks requiring integration of information.
Synergy increases as networks learn multiple diverse tasks.
In tasks requiring integration of multiple sources, performance critically relies on synergistic neurons.
Synergy is used to combine information from multiple modalities and supports flexible and efficient learning.
papers.limitation:
Use of relatively small networks and simple tasks.
Use of two specific PID measures (I_min and I_MMI) which do not have a clear operational interpretation.
Limited to feedforward and recurrent networks, not including more complex architectures like transformers.
future_direction: Disentangle the relevance of potential causes driving the reliance on synergistic neurons.
Investigate how synergy and redundancy trade off in larger, more complex networks and tasks.
Explore how different network architectures and learning algorithms influence the emergence of synergy.
papers.abstract: Striking progress has been made in understanding cognition by analyzing how the brain is engaged in different modes of information processing. For instance, so-called synergistic information (information encoded by a set of neurons but not by any subset) plays a key role in areas of the human brain linked with complex cognition. However, two questions remain unanswered: (a) how and why a cognitive system can become highly synergistic; and (b) how informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes. Here we employ an information-decomposition framework to investigate neural networks performing cognitive tasks. Our results show that synergy increases as networks learn multiple diverse tasks, and that in tasks requiring integration of multiple sources, performance critically relies on synergistic neurons. Overall, our results suggest that synergy is used to combine information from multiple modalities-and more generally for flexible and efficient learning. These findings reveal new ways of investigating how and why learning systems employ specific information-processing strategies, and support the principle that the capacity for general-purpose learning critically relies on the system's information dynamics.

papers.title: Unveiling Super Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is there a small subset of distinct experts that plays an exceptionally critical role in the underlying mechanisms of MoE LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper discovers and characterizes Super Experts (SEs), an exceptionally rare yet critical subset of experts in MoE LLMs, and shows they are the primary source of systematic outliers and attention sinks, with pruning them causing severe performance collapse.
papers.conclusion: Super Experts are a fundamental component of MoE LLMs, acting as the primary source of systematic outliers and attention sinks, and their compression severely degrades model performance by disrupting these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Super Experts (SEs) are a small subset of experts (less than 0.5%) that produce extreme activation outliers in the down_proj, leading to massive activations (MAs) in hidden states.
Pruning SEs causes a dramatic performance drop, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks (e.g., Pass@1 drops to nearly zero).
The distribution of SEs is model-specific, data-agnostic, and remains unchanged after post-training processes.
SEs are the primary source of systematic outliers in MoE LLMs, and their strong activation on attention sink tokens is crucial for the attention mechanism.
Compressing SEs disrupts the formation of attention sinks, leading to the collapse of the attention score distribution and model performance.
future_direction: Designing more expert-balanced pre-training regimes.
Advancing robust expert compression strategies.
papers.abstract: In this study, we report, for the first time, the discovery and systematic investigation of a distinct subset of experts that play a pivotal role in the MoE LLMs' forward inference. These experts are prevalent in open-source MoE LLMs, and despite their extremely limited number, pruning them results in a substantial decline in model performance (e.g., prune just three out of 6,144 causes Qwen3-30B-A3B to generate repetitive and uninformative outputs).We refer to these experts as Super Experts (SEs). Our comprehensive analysis provides progressively deeper insights into SEs: (i) SEs are characterized by rare but extreme activation outliers in the output of the down_proj, which give rise to massive activations in the hidden states between decoder layers. Moreover, the distribution of SEs is model-specific, data-agnostic, and remains unaffected by post-training processes. (ii) By pruning SEs, we assess their significance across a variety of tasks, revealing their considerable impact on the model's overall performance, particularly in mathematical reasoning. (iii) We further investigate why compressing SEs exerts such a pronounced impact. We show that, in MoE LLMs, SEs serve as the primary source of the systematic outlier mechanism in Transformers, and that compressing them profoundly disrupts this process, ultimately causing the collapse of attention sinks. These findings advance the understanding of the internal dynamics of MoE LLMs, filling an important gap in the current knowledge. The code is provided in https://github.com/ZunhaiSu/Super-Experts-Profilling.

papers.title: Distillation Dynamics: Towards Understanding Feature-Based Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-based knowledge distillation, which works well for CNNs, fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), and what is the root cause of negative transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern (compression followed by expansion) and identifies a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models as the root cause of negative transfer in feature-based distillation, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViT compression strategies.
papers.conclusion: Successful knowledge transfer in Vision Transformers requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect the fundamental representational constraints and the U-shaped information processing dynamics of these architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT models exhibit a learned U-shaped pattern in information entropy and activation magnitude across layers, indicating an initial compression phase followed by a task-specific expansion phase.
The failure of feature-based distillation in ViTs stems from a representational mismatch: teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity.
Late-layer feature alignment actively harms student performance (negative transfer) because it forces the student to adopt a representational paradigm incompatible with its capacity, disrupting its natural learning progression.
Frequency spectrum analysis shows teacher ViTs transition from low-pass to uniform, high-energy spectra in late layers, while CNNs maintain low-pass spectra, explaining why feature mimicry works for CNNs but fails for ViTs.
The U-shaped information processing signature is a consistent learned behavior across different ViT architectures (e.g., CaiT, standard ViT) and training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised like MAE).
papers.abstract: While feature-based knowledge distillation has proven highly effective for compressing CNNs, these techniques unexpectedly fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), often performing worse than simple logit-based distillation. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of this phenomenon through a novel analytical framework termed as "distillation dynamics", combining frequency spectrum analysis, information entropy metrics, and activation magnitude tracking. Our investigation reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern: initial compression followed by expansion. We identify the root cause of negative transfer in feature distillation: a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models. Through frequency-domain analysis, we show that teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding strategies in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity. This mismatch causes late-layer feature alignment to actively harm student performance. Our findings reveal that successful knowledge transfer in ViTs requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect these fundamental representational constraints, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViTs compression strategies. All source code and experimental logs are provided at https://github.com/thy960112/Distillation-Dynamics.

papers.title: How a student becomes a teacher: learning and forgetting through Spectral methods
papers.research_question: Can an invariant subnetwork be identified in an overparameterized student network that mimics a teacher network, and can a spectral optimization method achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: A spectral training method that, with regularization, identifies an invariant subnetwork within an overparameterized student network that mirrors the teacher's structure and retains full performance when pruned.
papers.conclusion: The spectral training method enables identification of a minimal, efficient subnetwork that retains performance and recovers the teacher's topological features, outperforming conventional weight decay and parametrization.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral method with regularization identifies an invariant subnetwork in the student that matches the teacher's size.
Pruning based on eigenvalue magnitude does not degrade performance until the invariant core is removed, exhibiting a phase-transition-like behavior.
The path distribution of the pruned student matches that of the teacher, unlike conventionally trained networks.
The method generalizes to various datasets (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR-100) and architectures (e.g., ResNet50).
The spectral parametrization yields a node importance ranking via eigenvalues, enabling effective structural pruning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments employ straightforward student network architectures; more complex architectures need to be tested for general conclusions.
The method has been validated on relatively simple datasets; generalization to more complex, real-world datasets is an open question.
The analysis focuses on ranking nodes in hidden layers; input neurons are not included, which could provide insights on relevant features.
future_direction: Extending the parametrization techniques to more advanced network architectures.
Testing the proposed techniques on larger and more complex real-world datasets.
Including input neurons in the analysis to identify key relevant features.
papers.abstract: In theoretical ML, the teacher-student paradigm is often employed as an effective metaphor for real-life tuition. The above scheme proves particularly relevant when the student network is overparameterized as compared to the teacher network. Under these operating conditions, it is tempting to speculate that the student ability to handle the given task could be eventually stored in a sub-portion of the whole network. This latter should be to some extent reminiscent of the frozen teacher structure, according to suitable metrics, while being approximately invariant across different architectures of the student candidate network. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art conventional learning techniques could not help in identifying the existence of such an invariant subnetwork, due to the inherent degree of non-convexity that characterizes the examined problem. In this work, we take a leap forward by proposing a radically different optimization scheme which builds on a spectral representation of the linear transfer of information between layers. The gradient is hence calculated with respect to both eigenvalues and eigenvectors with negligible increase in terms of computational and complexity load, as compared to standard training algorithms. Working in this framework, we could isolate a stable student substructure, that mirrors the true complexity of the teacher in terms of computing neurons, path distribution and topological attributes. When pruning unimportant nodes of the trained student, as follows a ranking that reflects the optimized eigenvalues, no degradation in the recorded performance is seen above a threshold that corresponds to the effective teacher size. The observed behavior can be pictured as a genuine second-order phase transition that bears universality traits.

papers.title: Bayesian Mixture-of-Experts: Towards Making LLMs Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: How can we improve the uncertainty quantification and calibration of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models by replacing the deterministic routing mechanism with a Bayesian one?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a Bayesian Mixture-of-Experts routing framework that models uncertainty in the routing decision, leading to improved calibration, routing stability, and out-of-distribution detection in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian MoE routing framework provides a practical and effective pathway to create more robust and self-aware LLMs by improving their internal uncertainty quantification.
papers.key_findings:
Bayesian routing methods significantly improve in-distribution calibration metrics (e.g., ECE, NLL) compared to deterministic routing.
Router-level uncertainty signals from Bayesian methods (e.g., inferred logit variance) are effective for out-of-distribution detection.
The proposed framework improves routing stability under input perturbations.
The Full-Covariance Variational Router (FCVR) and Mean-Field Variational Router (MFVR) often achieve the best calibration and OoD detection performance.
The Bayesian routing methods introduce manageable computational and memory overhead, making them practical for deployment.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead of some Bayesian methods (e.g., deep ensembles) can be non-trivial.
Experiments are limited to a single MoE model architecture (IBM Granite) and multiple-choice QA tasks.
future_direction: Extend the Bayesian routing framework to other model architectures and modalities.
Explore more efficient Bayesian inference techniques to reduce computational cost.
Apply and evaluate the framework on a broader range of tasks beyond multiple-choice QA.
papers.abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has enabled the creation of massive yet efficient Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the standard deterministic routing mechanism presents a significant limitation: its inherent brittleness is a key contributor to model miscalibration and overconfidence, resulting in systems that often do not know what they don't know. This thesis confronts this challenge by proposing a structured \textbf{Bayesian MoE routing framework}. Instead of forcing a single, deterministic expert selection, our approach models a probability distribution over the routing decision itself. We systematically investigate three families of methods that introduce this principled uncertainty at different stages of the routing pipeline: in the \textbf{weight-space}, the \textbf{logit-space}, and the final \textbf{selection-space}. Through a series of controlled experiments on a 3-billion parameter MoE model, we demonstrate that this framework significantly improves routing stability, in-distribution calibration, and out-of-distribution (OoD) detection. The results show that by targeting this core architectural component, we can create a more reliable internal uncertainty signal. This work provides a practical and computationally tractable pathway towards building more robust and self-aware LLMs, taking a crucial step towards making them know what they don't know.

papers.title: Sparsity and Superposition in Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: Do Mixture of Experts (MoEs) exhibit less superposition than dense models, do they show discrete phase changes in superposition based on feature sparsity/importance, and can expert specialization be understood through feature representation rather than load balancing?
papers.core_contribution: MoEs exhibit greater monosemanticity (less superposition) than dense models and do not show sharp phase changes; network sparsity, not feature sparsity/importance, better characterizes MoEs. A new feature-based definition of expert specialization shows experts naturally organize around coherent features with appropriate initialization.
papers.conclusion: MoEs exhibit greater monosemanticity than dense networks without phase changes, and experts naturally organize around coherent features when initialization encourages specialization, challenging the assumption that interpretability and capability are fundamentally at odds.
papers.key_findings:
MoEs do not exhibit sharp phase changes in superposition like dense models, showing more continuous transitions.
MoEs consistently exhibit greater monosemanticity (less superposition) than dense models with equivalent active and total parameters.
Experts in MoEs naturally organize around coherent feature combinations when initialization encourages specialization, based on monosemantic feature representation rather than load balancing.
Network sparsity (ratio of active to total experts) better characterizes MoEs than feature sparsity or importance.
MoEs achieve comparable loss to dense models while maintaining more interpretable (monosemantic) representations.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted in controlled toy-model settings, abstracting away complexities of large-scale transformers and realistic routing dynamics.
Architectural and routing choices are restricted (simple experts, fixed top-k routing, no auxiliary load-balancing losses).
Feature distributions in synthetic tasks are significantly simpler than those in natural data.
Downstream performance trade-offs, training stability, and specialization dynamics at scale are not evaluated.
future_direction: Explore what favors monosemanticity in MoEs.
Investigate how training dynamics of MoEs differ from those of the dense model.
Examine when specialization emerges.
Validate findings in large, realistic MoE systems.
papers.abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) models have become central to scaling large language models, yet their mechanistic differences from dense networks remain poorly understood. Previous work has explored how dense models use \textit{superposition} to represent more features than dimensions, and how superposition is a function of feature sparsity and feature importance. MoE models cannot be explained mechanistically through the same lens. We find that neither feature sparsity nor feature importance cause discontinuous phase changes, and that network sparsity (the ratio of active to total experts) better characterizes MoEs. We develop new metrics for measuring superposition across experts. Our findings demonstrate that models with greater network sparsity exhibit greater \emph{monosemanticity}. We propose a new definition of expert specialization based on monosemantic feature representation rather than load balancing, showing that experts naturally organize around coherent feature combinations when initialized appropriately. These results suggest that network sparsity in MoEs may enable more interpretable models without sacrificing performance, challenging the common assumption that interpretability and capability are fundamentally at odds.

papers.title: Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to enhance the deployment efficiency of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) by introducing plug-and-play expert-level sparsification techniques (expert pruning and skipping)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces post-training expert pruning and dynamic skipping methods for MoE LLMs, which significantly reduce memory usage and increase inference speed while maintaining model performance across a wide range of tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed post-training expert pruning and dynamic skipping methods can significantly reduce memory usage and enhance inference speed for MoE LLMs while maintaining high model performance, offering efficient deployment solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Expert pruning can reduce the number of GPUs needed for deployment (e.g., from 2 to 1 A100-80G GPU for Mixtral 8x7B) and achieve up to 1.27× inference speedup with a 2.9-point performance drop on average for task-agnostic models.
Using domain-specific calibration data (e.g., MATH) for expert pruning leads to better performance on corresponding downstream tasks compared to using general pre-training data (C4).
Dynamic expert skipping further enhances inference speed (up to 1.33×) with negligible performance drops when combined with expert pruning.
Fine-tuning pruned models on domain-specific data (e.g., MetaMathQA) can greatly reduce the performance gap between pruned and original models, and in some cases, pruned models can even outperform the original model after fine-tuning.
The proposed expert pruning method outperforms weight pruning methods like Wanda (2:4 sparsity) in terms of memory reduction, inference speed, and benchmark performance.
papers.limitation:
The expert pruning method is based on enumeration of expert combinations, which becomes cumbersome for MoE models with a large number of experts (e.g., 32) per layer.
Experiments are conducted only on Mixtral 8x7B and Mixtral 8x7B Instruct models; generalizability to other MoE LLMs remains to be verified.
future_direction: Further refine the pruning and skipping techniques.
Incorporate the methods with weight pruning or parameter quantization strategies for more effective deployment of MoE LLMs.
papers.abstract: Xudong Lu, Qi Liu, Yuhui Xu, Aojun Zhou, Siyuan Huang, Bo Zhang, Junchi Yan, Hongsheng Li. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: On Explaining Knowledge Distillation: Measuring and Visualising the Knowledge Transfer Process
papers.research_question: How to explain and quantify the knowledge transfer process in knowledge distillation, specifically visualizing distilled and residual features.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniCAM, a gradient-based visual explanation method for knowledge distillation, and two metrics (FSS and RS) to quantify the similarity and relevance of distilled knowledge.
papers.conclusion: UniCAM and the FSS and RS metrics provide valuable insights for explaining the knowledge distillation process, as demonstrated on various datasets.
papers.key_findings:
With Teacher guidance, Student models learn more relevant features and discard irrelevant ones, with distilled features focusing on key object parts and residual features on backgrounds.
UniCAM effectively visualizes distilled and residual features, showing that KD is not simple feature copying but guided training.
The proposed FSS and RS metrics quantify attention pattern similarity and feature relevance, showing higher RS for Students trained with KD.
Capacity gaps between Teacher and Student can impede knowledge transfer, but Teacher assistants can bridge this gap.
Experiments on multiple datasets and KD techniques validate the effectiveness of UniCAM and the metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were exclusively conducted on classification tasks.
Added computational cost from computing pairwise distances, gradients, and metrics.
future_direction: Extend UniCAM to more complex datasets.
Explore applicability to tasks beyond classification.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains challenging due to the opaque nature of the knowledge transfer process from a Teacher to a Student, making it difficult to address certain issues related to KD. To address this, we proposed UniCAM, a novel gradient-based visual explanation method, which effectively interprets the knowledge learned during KD. Our experimental results demonstrate that with the guidance of the Teacher's knowledge, the Student model becomes more efficient, learning more relevant features while discarding those that are not relevant. We refer to the features learned with the Teacher's guidance as distilled features and the features irrelevant to the task and ignored by the Student as residual features. Distilled features focus on key aspects of the input, such as textures and parts of objects. In contrast, residual features demonstrate more diffused attention, often targeting irrelevant areas, including the backgrounds of the target objects. In addition, we proposed two novel metrics: the feature similarity score (FSS) and the relevance score (RS), which quantify the relevance of the distilled knowledge. Experiments on the CIFAR10, ASIRRA, and Plant Disease datasets demonstrate that UniCAM and the two metrics offer valuable insights to explain the KD process.

papers.title: Toward universal steering and monitoring of AI models
papers.research_question: How can we extract linear representations of concepts from internal activations of AI models to enable steering and monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a scalable method using Recursive Feature Machines (RFM) to extract linear concept representations from internal model activations, enabling effective steering and monitoring across diverse models and concepts.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the power of using internal representations for steering and monitoring AI models, providing a cost-efficient alternative to fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
The RFM method can extract concept vectors that enable steering and monitoring in LLMs, VLMs, and reasoning models.
Concept vectors are transferable across languages and can be combined for multi-concept steering.
Newer, larger models are more steerable, and steering can improve model capabilities beyond standard prompting.
Concept representations are effective for monitoring misaligned content (hallucinations, toxic content) and outperform judge models.
The method is scalable, requiring under one minute and fewer than 500 training samples on a single GPU.
papers.abstract: Modern AI models contain much of human knowledge, yet understanding of their internal representation of this knowledge remains elusive. Characterizing the structure and properties of this representation will lead to improvements in model capabilities and development of effective safeguards. Building on recent advances in feature learning, we develop an effective, scalable approach for extracting linear representations of general concepts in large-scale AI models (language models, vision-language models, and reasoning models). We show how these representations enable model steering, through which we expose vulnerabilities, mitigate misaligned behaviors, and improve model capabilities. Additionally, we demonstrate that concept representations are remarkably transferable across human languages and combinable to enable multi-concept steering. Through quantitative analysis across hundreds of concepts, we find that newer, larger models are more steerable and steering can improve model capabilities beyond standard prompting. We show how concept representations are effective for monitoring misaligned content (hallucinations, toxic content). We demonstrate that predictive models built using concept representations are more accurate for monitoring misaligned content than using models that judge outputs directly. Together, our results illustrate the power of using internal representations to map the knowledge in AI models, advance AI safety, and improve model capabilities.

papers.title: It's not a Lottery, it's a Race: Understanding How Gradient Descent Adapts the Network's Capacity to the Task
papers.research_question: How does gradient descent reduce the theoretical capacity of neural networks to an effective capacity that fits the task, and how does this explain the lottery ticket conjecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient descent reduces effective capacity through three dynamical principles (mutual alignment, unlocking, racing), explaining how lottery tickets are selected via a race rather than a static lottery.
papers.conclusion: Gradient descent selects lottery tickets through a dynamical race where early-aligned neurons grow exponentially and inhibit others, reducing effective capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons align their weight vectors to task-relevant directions (mutual alignment) early in training before the loss drops.
Neurons that are closer to their target direction experience exponential growth in norm (unlocking), leading to a winner-takes-all dynamic.
Early-aligned neurons reduce the loss and gradients, inhibiting the growth of other neurons (racing), resulting in sparsity.
The lottery ticket conjecture is explained as a dynamical race: neurons with favorable initial alignment win and obtain higher norms.
Effective capacity is reduced through merging of aligned neurons or pruning of low-norm weights, corresponding to the discovered lottery tickets.
papers.limitation: Fully predicting lottery tickets early in training is not possible due to asynchronous learning speeds of different neuron groups and changes in target directions after the loss drops.
papers.abstract: Our theoretical understanding of neural networks is lagging behind their empirical success. One of the important unexplained phenomena is why and how, during the process of training with gradient descent, the theoretical capacity of neural networks is reduced to an effective capacity that fits the task. We here investigate the mechanism by which gradient descent achieves this through analyzing the learning dynamics at the level of individual neurons in single hidden layer ReLU networks. We identify three dynamical principles -- mutual alignment, unlocking and racing -- that together explain why we can often successfully reduce capacity after training through the merging of equivalent neurons or the pruning of low norm weights. We specifically explain the mechanism behind the lottery ticket conjecture, or why the specific, beneficial initial conditions of some neurons lead them to obtain higher weight norms.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers? Specifically, can we identify specific neurons responsible for expressing factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'knowledge neurons' and a gradient-based attribution method to identify neurons in feed-forward networks that express specific factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons within feed-forward networks, and these 'knowledge neurons' can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed method are positively correlated with the expression of their corresponding facts, as shown by suppression and amplification experiments.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts that express the correct relation compared to prompts that do not.
Knowledge neurons for a fact are largely exclusive to that fact, with minimal overlap between facts of different relations.
Preliminary case studies show that directly modifying parameters associated with knowledge neurons can update or erase specific factual knowledge with moderate impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
The method uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain unexplored.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Extend the method to multi-word blanks.
Explore how knowledge neurons work in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/ Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: LEMoE: Advanced Mixture of Experts Adaptor for Lifelong Model Editing of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we perform lifelong model editing effectively while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, inconsistent routing, and order sensitivity in Mixture of Experts adaptors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LEMoE, an advanced MoE adaptor for lifelong model editing that uses module insertion, KV anchor routing, and clustering-based order planning to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, inconsistent routing, and order sensitivity.
papers.conclusion: Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of LEMoE in lifelong editing, surpassing previous model editing techniques while maintaining outstanding performance in batch editing.
papers.key_findings:
Conventional MoE adaptor suffers from catastrophic forgetting in lifelong editing.
Conventional MoE adaptor exhibits inconsistent routing between training and inference stages in lifelong editing.
Editing order significantly impacts model performance (order sensitivity).
LEMoE outperforms previous model editing methods in lifelong editing tasks.
LEMoE maintains excellent performance in batch editing tasks.
papers.limitation:
LEMoE can fail in some editing cases, such as partial token errors, complete factual failures, and generalization failures.
Due to computational constraints, the number of experts is limited (max 5 in experiments).
future_direction: Mitigating failure cases of LEMoE
Optimizing editing instructions (modifying the editing context)
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require continual knowledge updates to stay abreast of the ever-changing world facts, prompting the formulation of lifelong model editing task. While recent years have witnessed the development of various techniques for single and batch editing, these methods either fail to apply or perform sub-optimally when faced with lifelong editing. In this paper, we introduce LEMoE, an advanced Mixture of Experts (MoE) adaptor for lifelong model editing. We first analyze the factors influencing the effectiveness of conventional MoE adaptor in lifelong editing, including catastrophic forgetting, inconsistent routing and order sensitivity. Based on these insights, we propose a tailored module insertion method to achieve lifelong editing, incorporating a novel KV anchor routing to enhance routing consistency between training and inference stage, along with a concise yet effective clustering-based editing order planning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in lifelong editing, surpassing previous model editing techniques while maintaining outstanding performance in batch editing task. Our code will be available.

papers.title: Knowledge Entropy Decay during Language Model Pretraining Hinders New Knowledge Acquisition
papers.research_question: How does a model's tendency to integrate parametric knowledge evolve during pretraining, and how does this affect knowledge acquisition and forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge entropy decreases during pretraining, which impairs the model's ability to acquire and retain new knowledge, and shows that resuscitating inactive memory vectors can mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Decreasing knowledge entropy during pretraining hinders knowledge acquisition and retention, and mid-stage models are optimal for further training to incorporate new knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge entropy consistently declines as pretraining advances.
Lower knowledge entropy correlates with reduced knowledge acquisition and increased forgetting.
Artificially increasing the activity of inactive memory vectors enhances knowledge acquisition and retention.
Mid-stage pretraining models strike the best balance for knowledge acquisition and retention.
The trend is consistent across model sizes and hyperparameters.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to OLMo models, and extending to other models is needed.
Resuscitation method may impair performance when applied to models with not sufficiently low knowledge entropy.
future_direction: Extending the investigation to other models beyond OLMo.
Developing more refined methods for resuscitating model parameters that preserve language modeling capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate how a model's tendency to broadly integrate its parametric knowledge evolves throughout pretraining, and how this behavior affects overall performance, particularly in terms of knowledge acquisition and forgetting. We introduce the concept of knowledge entropy, which quantifies the range of memory sources the model engages with; high knowledge entropy indicates that the model utilizes a wide range of memory sources, while low knowledge entropy suggests reliance on specific sources with greater certainty. Our analysis reveals a consistent decline in knowledge entropy as pretraining advances. We also find that the decline is closely associated with a reduction in the model's ability to acquire and retain knowledge, leading us to conclude that diminishing knowledge entropy (smaller number of active memory sources) impairs the model's knowledge acquisition and retention capabilities. We find further support for this by demonstrating that increasing the activity of inactive memory sources enhances the model's capacity for knowledge acquisition and retention.

papers.title: Probing Semantic Routing in Large Mixture-of-Expert Models
papers.research_question: Does expert routing in large mixture-of-expert (MoE) models exhibit semantic specialization based on input meaning?
papers.core_contribution: Provides systematic evidence that expert routing in modern MoE language models is sensitive to semantic content, showing higher expert overlap when meaning is preserved across inputs.
papers.conclusion: Expert routing in modern MoE models is sensitive to semantic content, with semantic specialization being a learned, emergent behavior that challenges assumptions that routing is primarily token-based.
papers.key_findings:
Expert overlap is significantly higher when target words have the same sense versus different senses across all tested models.
Semantic routing signals are strongest in the middle layers of the models.
Larger models generally exhibit stronger semantic routing signals, with Llama-4 Scout being an exception.
DeepSeek-R1 exhibits the clearest and most consistent semantic specialization pattern among the models studied.
SAE analysis reveals that experts also specialize by reasoning patterns (cognitive patterns) in addition to lexical semantics.
papers.limitation:
Limited coverage of the MoE design space due to reliance on a small set of publicly available models
Variation in training regimes may influence routing behavior but is difficult to disentangle due to incomplete documentation
papers.abstract: In the past year, large (>100B parameter) mixture-of-expert (MoE) models have become increasingly common in the open domain. While their advantages are often framed in terms of efficiency, prior work has also explored functional differentiation through routing behavior. We investigate whether expert routing in large MoE models is influenced by the semantics of the inputs. To test this, we design two controlled experiments. First, we compare activations on sentence pairs with a shared target word used in the same or different senses. Second, we fix context and substitute the target word with semantically similar or dissimilar alternatives. Comparing expert overlap across these conditions reveals clear, statistically significant evidence of semantic routing in large MoE models.

papers.title: On the Representation Collapse of Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: How can we prevent representation collapse in sparse mixture-of-experts (SMoE) models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the representation collapse issue in sparse mixture-of-experts (SMoE) models and proposes a routing algorithm that projects token and expert representations onto a low-dimensional hypersphere, alleviating collapse and improving performance and routing consistency.
papers.conclusion: The proposed routing algorithm effectively addresses representation collapse in SMoE models, leading to improved performance and more consistent routing.
papers.key_findings:
X-MOE consistently outperforms baseline SMoE models on cross-lingual language model pre-training and fine-tuning across multiple benchmarks.
X-MOE alleviates the representation collapse issue compared to the baseline, as shown by visualization and quantitative metrics.
X-MOE achieves more consistent routing behaviors during both pre-training and fine-tuning, with lower routing fluctuation and higher inter-run consistency.
The routing algorithm benefits from dimension reduction, L2 normalization, and freezing the router during fine-tuning.
X-MOE improves upstream masked language modeling perplexity compared to the baseline.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to language tasks; evaluation on vision and multimodal tasks is future work.
Scaling up model size is not reported; performance gain may be greater with more experts.
future_direction: Evaluate the proposed method on vision pretraining and multimodal pretraining.
Report the results of scaling up model size.
papers.abstract: Sparse mixture of experts provides larger model capacity while requiring a constant computational overhead. It employs the routing mechanism to distribute input tokens to the best-matched experts according to their hidden representations. However, learning such a routing mechanism encourages token clustering around expert centroids, implying a trend toward representation collapse. In this work, we propose to estimate the routing scores between tokens and experts on a low-dimensional hypersphere. We conduct extensive experiments on cross-lingual language model pre-training and fine-tuning on downstream tasks. Experimental results across seven multilingual benchmarks show that our method achieves consistent gains. We also present a comprehensive analysis on the representation and routing behaviors of our models. Our method alleviates the representation collapse issue and achieves more consistent routing than the baseline mixture-of-experts methods.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Inversion dynamics of class manifolds in deep learning reveals tradeoffs underlying generalisation
papers.research_question: How does the optimization dynamics balance segregation and entanglement of class manifolds during training, and what is the role of 'stragglers' in this tradeoff and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a non-monotonic dynamics in class manifold segregation during training, characterized by an inversion point where manifolds become more entangled, and identifies 'stragglers' as a subset of training examples that drive this inversion and are crucial for generalization.
papers.conclusion: The inversion dynamics reveals a tradeoff between segregation and entanglement of class manifolds, with stragglers playing a key role in shaping the learning dynamics and influencing generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Class manifold dynamics is non-monotonic: an initial segregation phase is followed by an inversion where manifolds expand and become more entangled.
The training error at the inversion point is stable across different optimizers, data subsets, and initializations.
The inversion is caused by 'stragglers', a set of misclassified examples at the inversion point, which are conserved across initializations and data shuffles.
Removing stragglers from the training set eliminates the inversion and leads to worse generalization.
The fraction of stragglers is an invariant property of the dataset, weakly dependent on architecture, and related to dataset complexity.
papers.limitation:
The phenomenology may not be as clear in state-of-the-art deep convolutional neural networks or transformers.
The analysis focuses solely on the internal representations at the first layer, even in deeper architectures.
The sensitivity of the test error under pruning to architecture choice is not fully explored.
future_direction: Exploring the relation between stragglers and other metrics of task difficulty, such as intrinsic dimensions of the dataset.
Investigating the potential role of stragglers in data pruning strategies and curriculum learning.
More systematic exploration of the behavior in different architectures, especially convolutional neural networks.
papers.abstract: To achieve near-zero training error in a classification problem, the layers of a feed-forward network have to disentangle the manifolds of data points with different labels, to facilitate the discrimination. However, excessive class separation can bring to overfitting since good generalisation requires learning invariant features, which involve some level of entanglement. We report on numerical experiments showing how the optimisation dynamics finds representations that balance these opposing tendencies with a non-monotonic trend. After a fast segregation phase, a slower rearrangement (conserved across data sets and architectures) increases the class entanglement.The training error at the inversion is stable under subsampling, and across network initialisations and optimisers, which characterises it as a property solely of the data structure and (very weakly) of the architecture. The inversion is the manifestation of tradeoffs elicited by well-defined and maximally stable elements of the training set, coined ``stragglers'', particularly influential for generalisation.

papers.title: Clustering units in neural networks: upstream vs downstream information
papers.research_question: How can we define and quantify modularity in neural networks? The paper investigates this by comparing upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity between hidden units.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that dropout increases modularity by making hidden units redundant, and that upstream and downstream definitions of functional similarity yield different clusters, indicating a misalignment between input-driven and output-driven neural representations.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that upstream and downstream ways of thinking about neural representations are not necessarily aligned, which has implications for representation learning and the definition of modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout dramatically increases modularity, contrary to the initial hypothesis that it would decrease modularity.
L2 regularization also increases modularity, while L1 regularization has a more modest effect.
Upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity agree within their families but disagree across families, leading to different cluster assignments.
The redundancy-inducing effect of dropout increases the clusterability of units.
Training increases cluster-similarity among upstream methods but not downstream methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to feedforward networks on MNIST, which may not have a meaningful modular solution.
Pairwise independence does not guarantee groupwise independence, which could be a limitation of the method.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks trained on more structured data, and to recurrent networks.
Evaluating the effect of maximizing modularity during training to see if it leads to performance benefits.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that some form of "modular" structure in artificial neural networks should be useful for learning, compositionality, and generalization. However, defining and quantifying modularity remains an open problem. We cast the problem of detecting functional modules into the problem of detecting clusters of similar-functioning units. This begs the question of what makes two units functionally similar. For this, we consider two broad families of methods: those that define similarity based on how units respond to structured variations in inputs ("upstream"), and those based on how variations in hidden unit activations affect outputs ("downstream"). We conduct an empirical study quantifying modularity of hidden layer representations of simple feedforward, fully connected networks, across a range of hyperparameters. For each model, we quantify pairwise associations between hidden units in each layer using a variety of both upstream and downstream measures, then cluster them by maximizing their "modularity score" using established tools from network science. We find two surprising results: first, dropout dramatically increased modularity, while other forms of weight regularization had more modest effects. Second, although we observe that there is usually good agreement about clusters within both upstream methods and downstream methods, there is little agreement about the cluster assignments across these two families of methods. This has important implications for representation-learning, as it suggests that finding modular representations that reflect structure in inputs (e.g. disentanglement) may be a distinct goal from learning modular representations that reflect structure in outputs (e.g. compositionality).

papers.title: Latent Neural Representations Analysis and Distillation for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we effectively distill Transformer models when there is a dimensionality mismatch between teacher and student, and how can analysis of latent neural representations (like outlier dimensions) inform better distillation algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces two novel distillation methods: Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) for handling mismatched attention heads between teacher and student models, and Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) which prioritizes critical outlier dimensions in latent representations. It also provides the first systematic analysis of emergent outlier dimensions in Encoder-Decoder T5 and instruction-finetuned Flan-T5 models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods for analyzing and distilling latent neural representations advance the understanding and acceleration of Transformer inference, with AMAD and EOFD demonstrating state-of-the-art distillation performance and generalization across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
AMAD enables effective distillation between teacher and student Transformers with different numbers of attention heads, outperforming conventional methods on vision-language tasks like VQA and captioning.
Outlier dimensions in T5 and Flan-T5 models, identified by unusually large activation magnitudes, are critical for zero-shot performance and are shared across layers within the encoder or decoder, but differ between encoder and decoder.
EOFD, which focuses distillation loss on these outlier dimensions, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GLUE benchmark and generalizes across BERT, GPT-2, and T5 architectures.
Distillation with AMAD can compensate for the absence of vision-language pre-training, and in some cases, distilled students outperform pre-trained and fine-tuned teachers.
The growth of outlier magnitude in T5 models is more correlated with increasing layer depth rather than overall model size, contrary to findings in GPT models.
papers.limitation: In some cases, a Teacher attention head may not be similar to any Student head after AMAD distillation, indicating a potential failure mode for knowledge transfer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-backed Large Language Models and Large Vision-Language Models are among the most widely used machine learning models recently. However, due to their enormous size, their behaviors and dynamics become difficult to understand and explain, and their inference speed and cost become slow and forbidding. Therefore, understanding their latent neural patterns and distilling their latent neural representations into smaller, cheaper, and faster models are vital for creating more explainable, accessible, and sustainable machine intelligence. However, knowledge distillation algorithms face an inherent challenge in minimizing the divergence between the neural activation representations of a teacher Transformer and a student Transformer: The latent representation spaces of the smaller Student always have lower dimensionality than those of the larger Teacher. We will address this Transformer distillation dimensionality mismatch or reduction problem by analyzing the neural activation patterns within these latent representation spaces and by proposing corresponding novel algorithms for distilling each group of components of Transformers. Our ultimate goal is to advance the field of understanding and accelerating the inference process of large Transformers by studying their latent neural representations.Specifically, we first develop novel algorithms for aligning the heads within the Multi-Head Attention components of these Transformers for latent neural representation distillation. We propose a new Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) method for Transformers with multi-head attention, which, unlike previous literature, can work for a Teacher and a Student with mismatched dimensionalities in terms of the numbers of attention heads. Specifically, we soft-align different heads in Teacher and Student attention maps using a cosine similarity weighting. The Teacher head contributes more to the Student heads for which it has a higher similarity weight. Each Teacher head contributes to all the Student heads by minimizing the divergence between the attention latent neural activation distributions for the soft-aligned heads.We then advance the understanding and distillation of the latent neural representations of the Feed Forward Network and Layer Normalization components of these Transformers. Previous literature shows that a small subset of dimensions within the high-dimensional latent neural representation spaces of language Transformers emerge as “outliers”, with weights or latent neuron activations of unusually large magnitudes—several standard deviations from the mean—during pretraining, and seem to encode critical linguistic knowledge in a sparse way. We systematically extend these previous findings on emergent outliers to Encoder-Decoder Transformers and instruction-finetuned models at scale, for the first time. We show that emergent outlier dimensions of the Transformer latent neural representations contribute significantly more to zero-shot performance than non-outlier dimensions. Leveraging our findings, we further propose the Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) method, which prioritizes these critical outlier latent dimensions to address the trade-off among these representation dimensions during distillation. Specifically, we propose a weighted MSE loss to place greater emphasis on the emergent outlier dimensions of the latent neural representations, which are identified by the standard deviations of neuron activation magnitudes.We demonstrate that our AMAD and EOFD distillation algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance empirically and generalize well to different Transformer architectures. Specifically, for AMAD, we experiment on distilling VL-T5 and BLIP and apply the AMAD loss to their T5, BERT, and ViT sub-modules. We show that, under vision-language settings, AMAD outperforms conventional distillation methods on the VQA-2.0, COCO captioning, and Multi30K translation datasets. We further show that even without VL pre-training, the distilled VL-T5 models outperform corresponding VL pre-trained VL-T5 models that are further fine-tuned by ground-truth signals, and that fine-tuning distillation can also compensate to some degree for the absence of VL pre-training in BLIP models. As for EOFD, we empirically show that it outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. We further demonstrate that EOFD generalizes well across Encoder-only BERT, Decoder-only GPT-2, and Encoder-Decoder T5 architectures.

papers.title: Representation Convergence: Mutual Distillation is Secretly a Form of Regularization
papers.research_question: What hinders reinforcement learning agents from generalizing like humans? How can we enable them to learn robust representations that drive human-like generalization behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies acts as an implicit regularization by improving policy robustness to irrelevant features, which leads to better generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mutual distillation is a form of implicit regularization that improves generalization in reinforcement learning by enhancing policy robustness to irrelevant features and promoting invariant representations.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, improving policy robustness to irrelevant features enhances generalization performance.
Empirically, mutual distillation (DML) improves generalization performance across Procgen environments.
DML leads to more robust representations that are invariant to irrelevant features, as visualized by t-SNE.
The proposed MDPO algorithm consistently outperforms the PPO baseline in generalization.
Ablation studies indicate the improvement is due to regularization against irrelevant features, not merely additional information sharing.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we argue that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies serves as an implicit regularization, preventing them from overfitting to irrelevant features. We highlight two separate contributions: (i) Theoretically, for the first time, we prove that enhancing the policy robustness to irrelevant features leads to improved generalization performance. (ii) Empirically, we demonstrate that mutual distillation between policies contributes to such robustness, enabling the spontaneous emergence of invariant representations over pixel inputs. Ultimately, we do not claim to achieve state-of-the-art performance but rather focus on uncovering the underlying principles of generalization and deepening our understanding of its mechanisms.

papers.title: On the Binding Problem in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the underlying cause for neural networks' shortcoming in human-level generalization? The paper argues it is the binding problem, the inability to dynamically and flexibly bind distributed information.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a unifying framework for the binding problem in neural networks, organizing it into three aspects: segregation (forming entities from inputs), representation (maintaining separation of information), and composition (using entities for inference).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a compositional approach to AI, based on grounded symbol-like representations, is fundamental for human-level generalization, and hopes this survey serves as a reference and inspiration for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks lack the ability to dynamically bind distributed information, which is crucial for compositional understanding and systematic generalization.
The binding problem can be divided into three functional aspects: segregation, representation, and composition.
Solving the binding problem requires incorporating inductive biases that enable symbolic processing to emerge within connectionist frameworks.
Existing mechanisms like attention, memory, and graph neural networks partially address aspects of the binding problem but a unified solution is still needed.
A unified approach within connectionism is preferable to hybrid neuro-symbolic systems for achieving human-level generalization.
papers.abstract: Contemporary neural networks still fall short of human-level generalization, which extends far beyond our direct experiences. In this paper, we argue that the underlying cause for this shortcoming is their inability to dynamically and flexibly bind information that is distributed throughout the network. This binding problem affects their capacity to acquire a compositional understanding of the world in terms of symbol-like entities (like objects), which is crucial for generalizing in predictable and systematic ways. To address this issue, we propose a unifying framework that revolves around forming meaningful entities from unstructured sensory inputs (segregation), maintaining this separation of information at a representational level (representation), and using these entities to construct new inferences, predictions, and behaviors (composition). Our analysis draws inspiration from a wealth of research in neuroscience and cognitive psychology, and surveys relevant mechanisms from the machine learning literature, to help identify a combination of inductive biases that allow symbolic information processing to emerge naturally in neural networks. We believe that a compositional approach to AI, in terms of grounded symbol-like representations, is of fundamental importance for realizing human-level generalization, and we hope that this paper may contribute towards that goal as a reference and inspiration.

papers.title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
papers.research_question: What gives rise to the illusion that individual neurons in BERT encode simple, consistent concepts when probed with a single dataset, and why does this interpretation fail to generalize across datasets?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an 'interpretability illusion' in BERT where neurons appear to encode simple concepts when probed with a single dataset, but these interpretations fail to generalize across datasets. It traces the illusion to dataset idiosyncrasy and local semantic coherence, and introduces a taxonomy of concept directions (global, dataset-level, local).
papers.conclusion: The work highlights the role of datasets in interpretability research and recommends testing interpretations across multiple datasets to avoid illusions. It also points to the need for further work in characterizing the geometry of concept representation.
papers.key_findings:
Many neurons in BERT's final layer show consistent, interpretable patterns when looking at top-activating sentences from a single dataset, but these patterns are not consistent across datasets.
The illusion arises because datasets occupy distinct regions of BERT's embedding space (dataset idiosyncrasy), as shown by UMAP visualization and linear SVM classification.
The patterns observed are largely due to local semantic coherence in the embedding space, not global concept directions, as evidenced by locality scores.
There exist both global and dataset-level concept directions in BERT's embedding space, as shown by monotonic token frequency changes along some neuron directions.
Annotator bias also contributes to the illusion, as people tend to see patterns even in random sentences.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the final layer of BERT; earlier layers are not fully analyzed.
Annotator bias can lead to seeing patterns where none exist.
future_direction: Replicate the analysis in other settings, such as with other sentence models, token-level embeddings, and earlier layers of BERT.
Look for similar illusions in other types of input like images and graphs.
Characterize the geometry of concept representation in more depth.
papers.abstract: We describe an "interpretability illusion" that arises when analyzing the BERT model. Activations of individual neurons in the network may spuriously appear to encode a single, simple concept, when in fact they are encoding something far more complex. The same effect holds for linear combinations of activations. We trace the source of this illusion to geometric properties of BERT's embedding space as well as the fact that common text corpora represent only narrow slices of possible English sentences. We provide a taxonomy of model-learned concepts and discuss methodological implications for interpretability research, especially the importance of testing hypotheses on multiple data sets.
