The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning Chains through Depth-Specialized Mixture-of-Experts in Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be made more efficient by adapting computational depth to input complexity using a mixture of depth-specialized experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DS-MoE, a transformer-based framework that dynamically allocates computational depth by composing specialized expert modules into reasoning chains, improving efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DS-MoE demonstrates that depth-adaptive expert selection can simultaneously improve efficiency, reasoning quality, and interpretability in large-scale language models.
papers.key_findings:
DS-MoE achieves up to 70% computational savings and 2x faster inference compared to uniform-depth transformers.
DS-MoE delivers higher accuracy (up to 5.3% improvement) on complex reasoning tasks like legal and long-context datasets.
The architecture reduces GPU memory footprint by 35-40% compared to baseline models.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of routing, memory integration experts, and meta-cognitive experts for performance.
DS-MoE generates more interpretable reasoning chains, offering transparency into the decision process.
papers.limitation:
The routing network introduces overhead that may impact latency, especially in real-time settings.
Effectiveness depends on the availability of suitably specialized expert modules, which may require domain-specific development and limit generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating reinforcement learning for routing optimization.
Introducing domain-specific experts.
Generalizing DS-MoE to multimodal reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Contemporary transformer architectures apply identical processing depth to all inputs, creating inefficiencies and limiting reasoning quality. Simple factual queries are subjected to the same multilayered computation as complex logical problems, wasting resources while constraining deep inference. To overcome this, we came up with a concept of Dynamic Reasoning Chains through Depth Specialised Mixture of Experts (DS-MoE), a modular framework that extends the Mixture of Experts paradigm from width-based to depth specialised computation. DS-MoE introduces expert modules optimised for distinct reasoning depths, shallow pattern recognition, compositional reasoning, logical inference, memory integration, and meta-cognitive supervision. A learned routing network dynamically assembles custom reasoning chains, activating only the necessary experts to match input complexity. The dataset on which we trained and evaluated DS-MoE is on The Pile, an 800GB corpus covering diverse domains such as scientific papers, legal texts, programming code, and web content, enabling systematic assessment across reasoning depths. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-MoE achieves up to 16 per cent computational savings and 35 per cent faster inference compared to uniform-depth transformers, while delivering 2.8 per cent higher accuracy on complex multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, routing decisions yield interpretable reasoning chains, enhancing transparency and scalability. These findings establish DS-MoE as a significant advancement in adaptive neural architectures, demonstrating that depth-specialised modular processing can simultaneously improve efficiency, reasoning quality, and interpretability in large-scale language models.

papers.title: Universal Properties of Activation Sparsity in Modern Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the universal properties of activation sparsity across diverse Large Language Model families and scales, and how does sparsity robustness vary with model size, training strategies, and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a general framework for evaluating activation sparsity robustness in LLMs, discovers that critical sparsity increases with model size, and presents the first study of activation sparsity in diffusion-based LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation sparsity is a universal property in modern LLMs with increasing relevance at scale, offering practical opportunities for efficiency gains and providing guidelines for future sparsity-aware model design.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate activations exhibit the highest tolerance to sparsity among FFN components.
Critical sparsity (the highest sparsity with ≤1% performance drop) tends to increase with model size across families.
Instruction-tuned models generally show greater tolerance to activation sparsity than their pretrained counterparts.
Activation sparsity patterns and robustness vary significantly across different downstream tasks.
In Mixture-of-Experts models, sparsity levels are consistent across experts within a layer, with low inter-expert variance.
papers.abstract: Activation sparsity is an intriguing property of deep neural networks that has been extensively studied in ReLU-based models, due to its advantages for efficiency, robustness, and interpretability. However, methods relying on exact zero activations do not directly apply to modern Large Language Models (LLMs), leading to fragmented, model-specific strategies for LLM activation sparsity and a gap in its general understanding. In this work, we introduce a general framework for evaluating sparsity robustness in contemporary LLMs and conduct a systematic investigation of this phenomenon in their feedforward~(FFN) layers. Our results uncover universal properties of activation sparsity across diverse model families and scales. Importantly, we observe that the potential for effective activation sparsity grows with model size, highlighting its increasing relevance as models scale. Furthermore, we present the first study of activation sparsity in diffusion-based LLMs. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive perspective and practical guidance for harnessing activation sparsity in LLM design and acceleration.

papers.title: Understanding Distributed Representations of Concepts in Deep Neural Networks without Supervision
papers.research_question: How can we understand the distributed representations of concepts in deep neural networks without supervision by selecting a principal subset of neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an unsupervised method for discovering distributed representations of concepts in deep neural networks by selecting a principal subset of neurons and constructing Relaxed Decision Regions (RDRs) using a novel Configuration distance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a way to understand learned concepts in DNNs without human supervision, and it can be used for various applications like subclass detection and misclassification reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Configuration distance effectively captures instances with similar concepts compared to Euclidean and Cosine distances.
The RDR framework can identify coherent concepts, including unlabeled subclasses, without human supervision.
The method can reason about misclassifications by identifying spurious correlations encoded in internal neurons.
The method reveals layer-wise differences in concept representations: lower layers capture spatial information, while higher layers capture class-specific features.
The method outperforms existing methods (KNN, CAR, CAV, RI) in terms of purity and entropy for subclass grouping on the Oxford-pet dataset.
papers.abstract: Understanding intermediate representations of the concepts learned by deep learning classifiers is indispensable for interpreting general model behaviors. Existing approaches to reveal learned concepts often rely on human supervision, such as pre-defined concept sets or segmentation processes. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised method for discovering distributed representations of concepts by selecting a principal subset of neurons. Our empirical findings demonstrate that instances with similar neuron activation states tend to share coherent concepts. Based on the observations, the proposed method selects principal neurons that construct an interpretable region, namely a Relaxed Decision Region (RDR), encompassing instances with coherent concepts in the feature space. It can be utilized to identify unlabeled subclasses within data and to detect the causes of misclassifications. Furthermore, the applicability of our method across various layers discloses distinct distributed representations over the layers, which provides deeper insights into the internal mechanisms of the deep learning model.

papers.title: Facts as Experts: Adaptable and Interpretable Neural Memory over Symbolic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we interface a neural language model with an interpretable symbolic memory to make knowledge accessible and modifiable without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural language model (Facts-as-Experts) with an explicit interface to a symbolic fact memory, enabling knowledge updates without retraining and improving performance on knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method for interfacing a neural language model with a symbolic memory, demonstrating improved QA performance and the ability to modify knowledge without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
FaE outperforms baseline models (FOFE, EmQL, EaE) on FreebaseQA and WebQuestionsSP QA datasets.
FaE can effectively answer questions using new facts injected into its memory at inference time without retraining.
FaE can update stale memories by overwriting facts, though performance decreases when new facts contradict pretraining data.
Removing overlapping entity pairs between pretraining/finetuning and test data reduces performance, indicating some memorization of paraphrases.
FaE shows a zero-shot capability, answering around a quarter of answerable questions without fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: Updating stale memories (where new facts contradict pretraining data) is more difficult and results in a performance drop, indicating the mixing between contextual representations and knowledge requires further research.
future_direction: Addressing the difficulty of updating stale memories and the problem of deleting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Massive language models are the core of modern NLP modeling and have been shown to encode impressive amounts of commonsense and factual information. However, that knowledge exists only within the latent parameters of the model, inaccessible to inspection and interpretation, and even worse, factual information memorized from the training corpora is likely to become stale as the world changes. Knowledge stored as parameters will also inevitably exhibit all of the biases inherent in the source materials. To address these problems, we develop a neural language model that includes an explicit interface between symbolically interpretable factual information and subsymbolic neural knowledge. We show that this model dramatically improves performance on two knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks. More interestingly, the model can be updated without re-training by manipulating its symbolic representations. In particular this model allows us to add new facts and overwrite existing ones in ways that are not possible for earlier models.

papers.title: A Note on Normalized Emergence Timing (in Pythia Language Model Evaluations)
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Pythia, a suite of 16 LLMs trained on public data in the same order with 154 checkpoints each, and provides tools to reconstruct exact training dataloaders, enabling controlled studies on training dynamics and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The highly controlled setup of the Pythia suite can yield novel insights into LLMs and their training dynamics, facilitating future research.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias can be reduced by swapping pronouns in the last portion of training, with larger models showing greater reduction.
Memorization follows a Poisson point process and is not influenced by the location of a sequence in the training data.
The impact of pretraining term frequencies on few-shot performance emerges after a phase change at 65,000 steps for models with 2.8B parameters or more.
papers.limitation: The noisiness in the progression of gender bias metrics may reflect actual changes or poor reliability of the CrowS-Pairs benchmark.
future_direction: Further study of interventions (modifying training data) for bias mitigation and other applications.
Investigation of the reliability of the CrowS-Pairs benchmark.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) develop and evolve over the course of training? How do these patterns change as models scale? To answer these questions, we introduce \textit{Pythia}, a suite of 16 LLMs all trained on public data seen in the exact same order and ranging in size from 70M to 12B parameters. We provide public access to 154 checkpoints for each one of the 16 models, alongside tools to download and reconstruct their exact training dataloaders for further study. We intend \textit{Pythia} to facilitate research in many areas, and we present several case studies including novel results in memorization, term frequency effects on few-shot performance, and reducing gender bias. We demonstrate that this highly controlled setup can be used to yield novel insights toward LLMs and their training dynamics. Trained models, analysis code, training code, and training data can be found at \url{https://github.com/EleutherAI/pythia}.

papers.title: On Semantic Cognition, Inductive Generalization, and Language Models
papers.research_question: What kinds of inductive generalizations about concepts are made by language models? To what extent do language models recognize and use emergent features during induction? How do the inductive generalization capacities of language models relate to their representational space?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an inductive reasoning-based framework to analyze semantic cognition and generalization in language models, drawing insights from cognitive science.
future_direction: Investigate inductive generalizations in language models
Study recognition and use of emergent features during induction
Analyze relationship between inductive generalization and representational space
papers.abstract: My doctoral research focuses on understanding semantic knowledge in neural network models trained solely to predict natural language (referred to as language models, or LMs), by drawing on insights from the study of concepts and categories grounded in cognitive science. I propose a framework inspired by 'inductive reasoning,' a phenomenon that sheds light on how humans utilize background knowledge to make inductive leaps and generalize from new pieces of information about concepts and their properties. Drawing from experiments that study inductive reasoning, I propose to analyze semantic inductive generalization in LMs using phenomena observed in human-induction literature, investigate inductive behavior on tasks such as implicit reasoning and emergent feature recognition, and analyze and relate induction dynamics to the learned conceptual representation space.

papers.title: Unveiling Instruction-Specific Neurons & Experts: An Analytical Framework for LLM's Instruction-Following Capabilities
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning reconfigure the internal computational mechanisms of LLMs to achieve superior instruction following?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SPARCOM framework to identify and analyze instruction-specific neurons and experts, revealing how fine-tuning shapes LLMs through sparse computational components.
papers.conclusion: This study provides novel insights into how instruction tuning shapes LLMs through sparse components, demonstrating how targeted modifications to these components significantly enhance instruction-following capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Identified instruction-specific neurons (ISNs) and experts (ISEs) that are crucial for processing and executing instructions.
ISNs and ISEs exhibit both generality (overlap across instruction types) and uniqueness (high similarity within the same instruction type).
The fundamental layer-wise distribution pattern of ISNs remains largely unchanged after fine-tuning, but the number of specialized ISNs increases.
Fine-tuning significantly alters the activation patterns of ISNs for the same instruction, while the activation of experts remains highly correlated.
Proposes a three-phase mechanistic framework (early, intermediate, final) to explain the operational principles of ISNs in both dense and MoE models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not develop strategies to leverage the identified instruction-specific components to enhance the model's instruction-following capabilities and task-solving performance.
The analysis is limited to six representative instruction types, which may not capture the full diversity of instructions.
future_direction: Explore larger and more diverse datasets to identify a broader range of Instruction-Specific Neurons and Experts, enhancing the generalizability of the findings.
papers.abstract: The finetuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced their instruction-following capabilities, yet the underlying computational mechanisms driving these improvements remain poorly understood. This study systematically examines how fine-tuning reconfigures LLM computations by isolating and analyzing instruction-specific sparse components, i.e., neurons in dense models and both neurons and experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. In particular, we introduce HexaInst, a carefully curated and balanced instructional dataset spanning six distinct categories, and propose SPARCOM, a novel analytical framework comprising three key contributions: (1) a method for identifying these sparse components, (2) an evaluation of their functional generality and uniqueness, and (3) a systematic comparison of their alterations. Through experiments, we demonstrate functional generality, uniqueness, and the critical role of these components in instruction execution. By elucidating the relationship between fine-tuning-induced adaptations and sparse computational substrates, this work provides deeper insights into how LLMs internalize instruction-following behavior for the trustworthy LLM community.

papers.title: Understanding the Behaviors of BERT in Ranking
papers.research_question: What are the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks on MS MARCO and TREC Web Track?
papers.core_contribution: BERT is effective for QA-focused passage ranking due to its interaction-based seq2seq matching, but less effective for ad hoc document ranking where user click signals are more beneficial.
papers.conclusion: BERT excels in seq2seq matching tasks like MS MARCO due to its pre-training on surrounding contexts, but for ad hoc document ranking, pre-training on user clicks is more effective.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-based rankers outperform previous neural IR models on MS MARCO passage ranking.
BERT is not effective as a representation-based model for ranking; it relies on cross-sequence interactions.
On TREC ad hoc ranking, BERT underperforms compared to feature-based learning to rank and models pre-trained on user clicks.
BERT's attention focuses on marker tokens and stopwords, but stopwords have minimal impact on performance.
BERT assigns extreme ranking scores and depends on a few key terms, preferring semantic matches over loose relevance.
papers.limitation: BERT performs worse on TREC ad hoc ranking compared to models pre-trained on user clicks, indicating a gap between its pre-training on surrounding contexts and the needs of document ranking.
future_direction: Training deeper networks on user clicks signals
Studying deeper models trained on relevance-based labels compared to shallower neural rankers
papers.abstract: This paper studies the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks. We explore several different ways to leverage the pre-trained BERT and fine-tune it on two ranking tasks: MS MARCO passage reranking and TREC Web Track ad hoc document ranking. Experimental results on MS MARCO demonstrate the strong effectiveness of BERT in question-answering focused passage ranking tasks, as well as the fact that BERT is a strong interaction-based seq2seq matching model. Experimental results on TREC show the gaps between the BERT pre-trained on surrounding contexts and the needs of ad hoc document ranking. Analyses illustrate how BERT allocates its attentions between query-document tokens in its Transformer layers, how it prefers semantic matches between paraphrase tokens, and how that differs with the soft match patterns learned by a click-trained neural ranker.

papers.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the hidden states in models of different scales? The paper investigates whether there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models trained on similar data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Linear Representation Transferability (LRT) Hypothesis and provides empirical evidence that affine mappings between hidden states of different-sized models can transfer steering vectors, enabling small models to steer large models.
papers.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence for the LRT hypothesis, suggesting that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the hypothesis is a promising direction for understanding representation alignment across model scales.
papers.key_findings:
Affine mappings can be learned between the hidden states of small and large models from the same family.
Steering vectors learned on small models retain their semantic effect when transferred to large models via the learned affine map.
The transferred steering vectors are as effective as those learned directly on the large model for tasks like refusal behavior removal and logit-based evaluation.
The feature spaces of models, as represented by sparse autoencoder decoder matrices, are approximately linearly related.
The conceptual framework of a universal representation space provides a plausible explanation for the linear transferability.
papers.limitation:
The limits of transferability across very different model sizes (e.g., 100M to 70B) are not yet understood.
Transferability across different model families or architectures is challenging due to differences in tokenization schemes and architectural design.
future_direction: Investigating the limits of transferability across model sizes.
Exploring transferability across different model families and architectures.
Developing theoretical foundations for the LRT hypothesis and the universal representation space.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that neural networks with similar architectures trained on similar data learn shared representations relevant to the learning task. We build on this idea by extending the conceptual framework where representations learned across models trained on the same data can be expressed as linear combinations of a \emph{universal} set of basis features. These basis features underlie the learning task itself and remain consistent across models, regardless of scale. From this framework, we propose the \textbf{Linear Representation Transferability (LRT)} Hypothesis -- that there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models. To test this hypothesis, we learn affine mappings between the hidden states of models of different sizes and evaluate whether steering vectors -- directions in hidden state space associated with specific model behaviors -- retain their semantic effect when transferred from small to large language models using the learned mappings. We find strong empirical evidence that such affine mappings can preserve steering behaviors. These findings suggest that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the LRT hypothesis may be a promising direction on understanding representation alignment across model scales.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: Interpreting Pretrained Contextualized Representations via Reductions to Static Embeddings
papers.research_question: Can we convert pretrained contextualized representations to static embeddings to leverage mature static embedding interpretability methods, and what do we learn about representational quality and social bias through this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces simple, general methods for converting contextualized representations to static embeddings, enabling the use of static embedding interpretability methods. Analysis reveals that pooling over many contexts improves representational quality and that social bias is encoded disparately across models and layers.
papers.conclusion: Converting contextualized representations to static embeddings is a viable approach for interpretability, revealing important insights about representational quality and bias, and enabling the use of mature static embedding analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Pooling over many contexts (aggregated strategy) significantly improves the representational quality of static embeddings derived from contextualized models.
The best-performing layer for static embeddings shifts to later layers as the number of contexts increases.
Static embeddings derived from contextualized models can outperform traditional static embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe on word similarity tasks.
Social bias is encoded disparately across different pretrained models and across different layers of the same model.
Existing bias estimators for word embeddings are dramatically inconsistent with each other.
papers.limitation:
The study only addresses a restricted subset of social biases and does not cover intersectional biases.
Existing bias estimators are inconsistent and may not reliably estimate bias.
future_direction: Investigate how the reduction to static embeddings affects different models and what it reflects about linguistic knowledge.
papers.abstract: Contextualized representations (e.g. ELMo, BERT) have become the default pretrained representations for downstream NLP applications. In some settings, this transition has rendered their static embedding predecessors (e.g. Word2Vec, GloVe) obsolete. As a side-effect, we observe that older interpretability methods for static embeddings -while more mature than those available for their dynamic counterparts -are underutilized in studying newer contextualized representations. Consequently, we introduce simple and fully general methods for converting from contextualized representations to static lookup-table embeddings which we apply to 5 popular pretrained models and 9 sets of pretrained weights. Our analysis of the resulting static embeddings notably reveals that pooling over many contexts significantly improves representational quality under intrinsic evaluation. Complementary to analyzing representational quality, we consider social biases encoded in pretrained representations with respect to gender, race/ethnicity, and religion and find that bias is encoded disparately across pretrained models and internal layers even for models that share the same training data. Concerningly, we find dramatic inconsistencies between social bias estimators for word embeddings.

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.

papers.title: Understanding and Leveraging the Expert Specialization of Context Faithfulness in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.research_question: Do context-faithful experts exist within MoE models, and how can they be leveraged for improved context faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Router Lens to identify context-faithful experts in MoE models and introduces CEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that matches or surpasses full fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Expert specialization for context faithfulness exists in MoE models, and CEFT effectively leverages this for efficient fine-tuning, yielding strong empirical gains while maintaining efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Router tuning significantly improves performance on context-dependent tasks, indicating the existence of context-faithful experts.
Masking context-faithful experts leads to substantial performance drops, confirming their importance.
Context-faithful experts amplify attention to relevant context and answer tokens in deeper layers.
CEFT matches or surpasses full fine-tuning while being more parameter-efficient.
The learned routing strategies generalize to unseen tasks.
papers.limitation: Router Lens cannot identify context-faithful experts in a zero-shot or training-free setting, and improving their context utilization ability depends on training procedures.
future_direction: Combining mechanistic interpretability techniques such as SAE to further unravel MoE experts.
Extending methods to other forms of specialization such as reflection and reasoning.
papers.abstract: Context faithfulness is essential for reliable reasoning in context-dependent scenarios. However, large language models often struggle to ground their outputs in the provided context, resulting in irrelevant responses. Inspired by the emergent expert specialization observed in mixture-of-experts architectures, this work investigates whether certain experts exhibit specialization in context utilization, offering a potential pathway toward targeted optimization for improved context faithfulness. To explore this, we propose Router Lens, a method that accurately identifies context-faithful experts. Our analysis reveals that these experts progressively amplify attention to relevant contextual information, thereby enhancing context grounding. Building on this insight, we introduce Context-faithful Expert Fine-Tuning (CEFT), a lightweight optimization approach that selectively fine-tunes context-faithful experts. Experiments across a wide range of benchmarks and models demonstrate that CEFT matches or surpasses the performance of full fine-tuning while being significantly more efficient.

papers.title: The Illusion of Specialization: Unveiling the Domain-Invariant "Standing Committee" in Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.research_question: Does a domain-invariant 'Standing Committee' of experts emerge in Mixture-of-Experts models, and what is its role in reasoning and domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a domain-invariant 'Standing Committee'—a compact coalition of experts that dominates routing mass across domains—in Mixture-of-Experts models, challenging the assumption of expert specialization and revealing a structural bias toward centralized computation.
papers.conclusion: MoE models rely on a domain-invariant Standing Committee that anchors reasoning and syntax, indicating centralized computation emerges from sparse routing itself, which challenges current training objectives like load-balancing losses.
papers.key_findings:
A domain-invariant Standing Committee of experts emerges across different MoE models and domains, capturing the majority of routing mass.
The committee is compact and stable across layers, with its size largely insensitive to routing budget changes.
Committee members anchor logical framing, reasoning control, and syntactic structure, while peripheral experts handle domain-specific knowledge.
Centralization is an emergent property of sparse routing, not just an architectural artifact, even in models with shared experts.
Standard load-balancing losses that enforce uniform expert utilization may conflict with this natural optimization path, limiting training efficiency.
papers.limitation:
Analysis covers only a small set of representative MoE architectures and settings, not spanning hybrid, hierarchical, or dynamically adaptive routing designs.
The study is observational and inference-only, without direct intervention in routing or causal effects measurement.
Evaluation primarily relies on domain-level analyses over MMLU, which may not fully capture behavior in conversational, multi-step reasoning, coding, or tool-augmented scenarios.
The framework focuses on routing statistics rather than training dynamics, leaving open how and when Standing Committees emerge during optimization.
future_direction: Incorporate targeted ablations and routing perturbations to measure causal effects.
Study training dynamics to understand when and how Standing Committees emerge during optimization.
Develop function-aware routing and architectures that explicitly support a core–periphery organization of expertise.
papers.abstract: Mixture of Experts models are widely assumed to achieve domain specialization through sparse routing. In this work, we question this assumption by introducing COMMITTEEAUDIT, a post hoc framework that analyzes routing behavior at the level of expert groups rather than individual experts. Across three representative models and the MMLU benchmark, we uncover a domain-invariant Standing Committee. This is a compact coalition of routed experts that consistently captures the majority of routing mass across domains, layers, and routing budgets, even when architectures already include shared experts. Qualitative analysis further shows that Standing Committees anchor reasoning structure and syntax, while peripheral experts handle domain-specific knowledge. These findings reveal a strong structural bias toward centralized computation, suggesting that specialization in Mixture of Experts models is far less pervasive than commonly believed. This inherent bias also indicates that current training objectives, such as load-balancing losses that enforce uniform expert utilization, may be working against the model's natural optimization path, thereby limiting training efficiency and performance.

papers.title: Integrated deep visual and semantic attractor neural networks predict fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway
papers.research_question: How does visual processing activate and interact with semantic representations during object recognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines a deep convolutional neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics and shows that different stages of this integrated model explain fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway.
papers.conclusion: The combined visuo-semantic model provides a proof-of-principle for how visual and semantic processing can be integrated and accounts for neural data along the ventral stream, showing a gradient from visual to semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Visual layers of the DNN best explain activation patterns in early visual cortex.
Posterior ventral temporal cortex is best explained by early stages of the semantic attractor network, corresponding to initial semantic processing.
Perirhinal cortex is best explained by the final stages of the semantic attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated.
The model learns associations between high-level visual regularities and semantic features, with shared semantic features activating more rapidly than distinctive features.
The model implements a general-to-specific account of object processing, where coarse-grained semantics activate before fine-grained details.
papers.limitation:
The model is trained in two separate stages (pre-trained DNN then attractor network), so there is no possibility for semantic representations to influence earlier visual layers via feedback.
The model is trained and tested on a specific set of images and has not been evaluated on its ability to generalize semantic patterns to previously unseen images.
future_direction: Training the visual and semantic components of the model together in an end-to-end manner.
Exploring architectures with direct connections from early visual layers to semantics, semantic-to-visual top-down connections, and lateral recurrent connections within visual layers.
Testing the model's semantic patterns for previously unseen images.
papers.abstract: Recognising an object involves rapid visual processing and activation of semantic knowledge about the object, but how visual processing activates and interacts with semantic representations remains unclear. Cognitive neuroscience research has shown that while visual processing involves posterior regions along the ventral stream, object meaning involves more anterior regions, especially perirhinal cortex. Here we investigate visuo-semantic processing by combining a deep neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics, such that visual information maps onto object meanings represented as activation patterns across features. In the combined model, concept activation is driven by visual input and co-occurrence of semantic features, consistent with neurocognitive accounts. We tested the model's ability to explain fMRI data where participants named objects. Visual layers explained activation patterns in early visual cortex, whereas pattern-information in perirhinal cortex was best explained by later stages of the attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated. Posterior ventral temporal cortex was best explained by intermediate stages corresponding to initial semantic processing, when visual information has the greatest influence on the emerging semantic representation. These results provide proof of principle of how a mechanistic model of combined visuo-semantic processing can account for pattern-information in the ventral stream.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: An Analysis of Attention Mechanisms: The Case of Word Sense Disambiguation in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How do encoder-decoder attention mechanisms handle ambiguous words in neural machine translation? Specifically, do they pay more attention to context tokens for disambiguation?
papers.core_contribution: Attention mechanisms in NMT do not primarily use context tokens for word sense disambiguation; instead, they focus more on the ambiguous word itself. Contextual information for disambiguation is encoded in the encoder hidden states. In Transformer models, early attention layers learn token alignment, while later layers learn to extract features from unaligned context tokens.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not the primary mechanism NMT models use for word sense disambiguation; contextual information is instead encoded in the encoder hidden states. Transformer attention mechanisms exhibit a layer-wise specialization for alignment and context feature extraction.
papers.key_findings:
Word sense disambiguation in NMT is challenging, with data sparsity being a main issue.
Attention mechanisms distribute more attention to the ambiguous noun itself rather than to context tokens when translating ambiguous nouns.
Encoder-decoder attention is not the main mechanism for incorporating contextual information for WSD; models encode this information in the encoder hidden states.
In Transformer attention mechanisms, the first few layers learn to align source and target tokens, while the last few layers learn to capture features from related but unaligned context tokens.
Higher attention weight on an ambiguous noun correlates with higher WSD accuracy.
papers.limitation: Automatic evaluation is limited by subword-level model outputs and imperfect alignment, which can cause correct translations to be misclassified.
future_direction: Deepening understanding of how NMT models internally represent word senses and similar phenomena.
Applying insights to transfer learning, translation error diagnosis, and designing architectures with document-level context windows.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that the encoderdecoder attention mechanisms in neural machine translation (NMT) are different from the word alignment in statistical machine translation. In this paper, we focus on analyzing encoder-decoder attention mechanisms, in the case of word sense disambiguation (WSD) in NMT models. We hypothesize that attention mechanisms pay more attention to context tokens when translating ambiguous words. We explore the attention distribution patterns when translating ambiguous nouns. Counterintuitively, we find that attention mechanisms are likely to distribute more attention to the ambiguous noun itself rather than context tokens, in comparison to other nouns. We conclude that attention is not the main mechanism used by NMT models to incorporate contextual information for WSD. The experimental results suggest that NMT models learn to encode contextual information necessary for WSD in the encoder hidden states. For the attention mechanism in Transformer models, we reveal that the first few layers gradually learn to "align" source and target tokens and the last few layers learn to extract features from the related but unaligned context tokens.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Unified View of Grokking, Double Descent and Emergent Abilities: A Perspective from Circuits Competition
papers.research_question: How can grokking, double descent, and emergent abilities be understood through a unified framework based on the competition between memorization and generalization circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that unifies grokking, double descent, and emergent abilities through the competition between memorization and generalization circuits, validated on algorithmic tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework based on memorization-generalization circuit competition successfully unifies grokking, double descent, and emergent abilities, offering a new perspective for understanding deep learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Critical dataset size for generalization decreases with model size.
Memorization capacity increases with model size.
Four distinct training dynamics (progression, ungrokking, grokking, semi-grokking) are identified based on model size and data size.
Double descent arises from the transition through progression, ungrokking, semi-grokking, and grokking as model size increases.
Emergent abilities can be induced by mixing memorization and generalization tasks in multi-task learning.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to algorithmic tasks and has not been validated on more realistic tasks or models.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more realistic tasks and models beyond algorithmic tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have uncovered intriguing phenomena in deep learning, such as grokking, double descent, and emergent abilities in large language models, which challenge human intuition and are crucial for a deeper understanding of neural models. In this paper, we present a comprehensive framework that provides a unified view of these three phenomena, focusing on the competition between memorization and generalization circuits. This approach, initially employed to explain grokking, is extended in our work to encompass a wider range of model sizes and training data volumes. Our framework delineates four distinct training dynamics, each depending on varying combinations of model size and training data quantity. Utilizing this framework, we provide a detailed analysis of the double descent phenomenon and propose two verifiable predictions regarding its occurrence, both substantiated by our experimental results. Moreover, we expand our framework to the multi-task learning paradigm, demonstrating how algorithm tasks can be turned into emergent abilities. This offers a novel perspective to understand emergent abilities in Large Language Models.

papers.title: Examining CNN Representations With Respect to Dataset Bias
papers.research_question: How to diagnose representation flaws in a pre-trained CNN caused by dataset bias, without using any testing samples?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to discover biased representations in a pre-trained CNN without testing samples by mining attribute relationships from internal inference patterns and comparing them to ground-truth relationships.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method effectively discovers representation flaws in CNNs caused by dataset bias and can guide the collection of new training samples to address these flaws.
papers.key_findings:
The method can identify attributes with biased representations even when the CNN achieves high accuracy on potentially biased testing samples.
The level of representation bias is not necessarily proportional to the level of dataset bias in the training data.
The method can discover both blind spots (where the CNN fails to encode expected relationships) and failure modes (where the CNN encodes incorrect relationships).
The method is more effective at discovering failure modes than a baseline method based on the entropy of annotation distributions.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to say all discovered representation biases are 'definitely' incorrect, as some may represent indirect relationships between attributes (e.g., using rosy cheeks to infer wearing lipstick).
future_direction: Encode ground-truth attribute relationships as a prior into the end-to-end learning of CNNs to achieve more reasonable representations.
papers.abstract: Given a pre-trained CNN without any testing samples, this paper proposes a simple yet effective method to diagnose feature representations of the CNN. We aim to discover representation flaws caused by potential dataset bias. More specifically, when the CNN is trained to estimate image attributes, we mine latent relationships between representations of different attributes inside the CNN. Then, we compare the mined attribute relationships with ground-truth attribute relationships to discover the CNN's blind spots and failure modes due to dataset bias. In fact, representation flaws caused by dataset bias cannot be examined by conventional evaluation strategies based on testing images, because testing images may also have a similar bias. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: On the Transferability of Representations in Neural Networks Between Datasets and Tasks
papers.research_question: How do representations in deep neural networks transfer layer-wise across different datasets and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks can be non-symmetric, is more influenced by dataset/task nature than architecture, and can quantify task relatedness.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of curriculum methods and structured approaches in multi-task learning paradigms to maximize knowledge transfer and minimize interference between datasets or tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise transferability between two datasets or tasks can be non-symmetric.
The nature of the datasets or tasks involved is more influential on transferability compared to neural network architecture.
Layer-wise transferability can be used as a proxy for quantifying task relatedness.
Initial layers in deep networks are more transferable than final layers.
Representations learned on more general datasets (e.g., CIFAR) are more transferable than those learned on specific datasets (e.g., SVHN).
papers.abstract: Deep networks, composed of multiple layers of hierarchical distributed representations, tend to learn low-level features in initial layers and transition to high-level features towards final layers. Paradigms such as transfer learning, multi-task learning, and continual learning leverage this notion of generic hierarchical distributed representations to share knowledge across datasets and tasks. Herein, we study the layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks across a few datasets and tasks and note some interesting empirical observations.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: Factorizing Knowledge in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a pretrained neural network be decomposed into task-wise disentangled factor networks that can be assembled without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Knowledge Factorization (KF), a method to decompose a pretrained teacher network into task-disentangled factor networks, each with a shared common-knowledge module and task-specific module, enabling plug-and-play assembly without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge Factorization effectively decomposes a pretrained teacher into task-disentangled factor networks that are modular, interpretable, and readily integratable, demonstrating strong performance and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
Factor networks achieve competitive or better predictive performance compared to knowledge distillation baselines on dedicated tasks.
Factor networks exhibit disentangled representations, as measured by various disentanglement metrics and representation similarity analysis.
The common-knowledge module learned via KF benefits transfer learning to unseen downstream tasks.
KF resolves the negative transfer problem in multi-task learning by structurally and representationally separating task-specific knowledge.
KF provides modularity and scalability, allowing the construction of combined-task networks by assembling factor networks without retraining.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we explore a novel and ambitious knowledge-transfer task, termed Knowledge Factorization~(KF). The core idea of KF lies in the modularization and assemblability of knowledge: given a pretrained network model as input, KF aims to decompose it into several factor networks, each of which handles only a dedicated task and maintains task-specific knowledge factorized from the source network. Such factor networks are task-wise disentangled and can be directly assembled, without any fine-tuning, to produce the more competent combined-task networks. In other words, the factor networks serve as Lego-brick-like building blocks, allowing us to construct customized networks in a plug-and-play manner. Specifically, each factor network comprises two modules, a common-knowledge module that is task-agnostic and shared by all factor networks, alongside with a task-specific module dedicated to the factor network itself. We introduce an information-theoretic objective, InfoMax-Bottleneck~(IMB), to carry out KF by optimizing the mutual information between the learned representations and input. Experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that, the derived factor networks yield gratifying performances on not only the dedicated tasks but also disentanglement, while enjoying much better interpretability and modularity. Moreover, the learned common-knowledge representations give rise to impressive results on transfer learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Adamdad/KnowledgeFactor.

papers.title: Granger-causal Attentive Mixtures of Experts: Learning Important Features with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can neural networks provide quantifiable measures of feature importance and the expected accuracy of their explanations, addressing the black-box criticism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attentive mixture of experts (AME) model that couples attentive gating with a Granger-causal objective to jointly produce accurate predictions and quantifiable measures of feature importance.
papers.conclusion: The AME model enables accurate predictions and quantifiable feature importance attributions, facilitating knowledge discovery from observational data without harming predictive performance.
papers.key_findings:
The AME provides quantifiable feature importance attributions that can be compared across decisions.
The Granger-causal objective prevents the collapse of attention weights (to a single expert or uniform) during training.
In medical prescription demand forecasting, the AME performed comparably to RNN and FNN baselines and better than ARIMA, while providing feature attributions.
For Parkinson's disease classification, the AME achieved a low classification error (7.69%) and identified relevant audio features.
For cancer type classification, the AME achieved high AUC (0.998) and identified discriminatory genes with links to specific cancers.
papers.limitation: Early during training, the attentive gating mechanism can collapse to assigning all attention to one expert or equal attention to all experts.
papers.abstract: Knowledge of the importance of input features towards decisions made by machine-learning models is essential to increase our understanding of both the models and the underlying data. Here, we present a new approach to estimating feature importance with neural networks based on the idea of distributing the features of interest among experts in an attentive mixture of experts (AME). AMEs use attentive gating networks trained with a Granger-causal objective to learn to jointly produce accurate predictions as well as estimates of feature importance in a single model. Our experiments show (i) that the feature importance estimates provided by AMEs compare favourably to those provided by state-of-the-art methods, (ii) that AMEs are significantly faster at estimating feature importance than existing methods, and (iii) that the associations discovered by AMEs are consistent with those reported by domain experts.

papers.title: An Interpretable Reasoning Network for Multi-Relation Question Answering
papers.research_question: How to perform interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning for multi-relation question answering over knowledge bases.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretable reasoning network for multi-relation question answering that provides traceable, hop-by-hop reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: The Interpretable Reasoning Network effectively answers multi-relation questions through an interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning process, providing traceable paths for analysis and manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
IRN outperforms baseline models on multiple QA datasets, including PathQuestion and WorldCup2014.
IRN provides interpretable intermediate predictions, enabling traceable reasoning paths and failure diagnosis.
IRN is robust to incomplete knowledge bases due to its multitask training schema.
The model allows manual manipulation of intermediate predictions to improve final answer accuracy.
IRN can map KB relations to natural language words, demonstrating its interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Representing questions as bag-of-words may be too simple; more sophisticated encoders like CNN or LSTM could be considered.
Cannot handle arithmetic operations or multi-constraint questions.
future_direction: Handling arithmetic operations in questions.
Handling multi-constraint questions.
Using more sophisticated encoders like CNN or LSTM for question representation.
papers.abstract: Multi-relation Question Answering is a challenging task, due to the requirement of elaborated analysis on questions and reasoning over multiple fact triples in knowledge base. In this paper, we present a novel model called Interpretable Reasoning Network that employs an interpretable, hop-by-hop reasoning process for question answering. The model dynamically decides which part of an input question should be analyzed at each hop; predicts a relation that corresponds to the current parsed results; utilizes the predicted relation to update the question representation and the state of the reasoning process; and then drives the next-hop reasoning. Experiments show that our model yields state-of-the-art results on two datasets. More interestingly, the model can offer traceable and observable intermediate predictions for reasoning analysis and failure diagnosis, thereby allowing manual manipulation in predicting the final answer.

papers.title: Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis
papers.research_question: Does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? This paper challenges the view of representational optimism by comparing the internal representations of networks trained via open-ended search versus conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
papers.core_contribution: The paper challenges representational optimism by introducing the Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) hypothesis, demonstrating that networks trained with conventional SGD can develop disorganized internal representations (FER) even when output performance is good, whereas networks from open-ended search can achieve more organized Unified Factored Representations (UFR).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Fractured Entangled Representation (FER) is a potential issue in conventional deep learning, raising questions about the adaptability of models trained via SGD, and that understanding and mitigating FER could be critical for the future of representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Networks trained with conventional SGD to produce a target image exhibit Fractured Entangled Representations (FER), where information for unitary concepts is split into disconnected, redundant pieces that become entangled.
Networks evolved through the open-ended Picbreeder process for the same output image exhibit Unified Factored Representations (UFR), where concepts are represented in a single, modular, and reusable manner.
Weight sweeps reveal that UFR networks allow for meaningful, human-recognizable variations (e.g., changing symmetry, stem angle) while respecting regularities, whereas FER networks produce deleterious, entangled changes that break regularities.
The path (curriculum) taken during learning influences the final representation; open-ended search discovers fundamental regularities (like symmetry) early, which are then elaborated upon, while conventional SGD takes a direct, greedy path.
The paper speculates that FER in large models may underlie challenges in generalization, creativity, and continual learning, and that the order in which concepts are learned is fundamental to the quality of the internal representation.
papers.limitation:
The study is conducted on a minimal, toy task (generating a single image) using CPPNs/MLPs, which is far simpler than large-scale models like LLMs.
The implications of FER for large models are speculative and based on analogy and limited examples of LLM behavior.
future_direction: Investigate FER in large models like LLMs and explore ways to mitigate it.
Study the impact of curricula and the ordering of concepts during training on the development of FER/UFR.
Explore alternative training algorithms and objectives (e.g., open-ended, novelty-seeking) that might lead to better internal representations.
papers.abstract: Much of the excitement in modern AI is driven by the observation that scaling up existing systems leads to better performance. But does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? While the representational optimist assumes it must, this position paper challenges that view. We compare neural networks evolved through an open-ended search process to networks trained via conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the simple task of generating a single image. This minimal setup offers a unique advantage: each hidden neuron's full functional behavior can be easily visualized as an image, thus revealing how the network's output behavior is internally constructed neuron by neuron. The result is striking: while both networks produce the same output behavior, their internal representations differ dramatically. The SGD-trained networks exhibit a form of disorganization that we term fractured entangled representation (FER). Interestingly, the evolved networks largely lack FER, even approaching a unified factored representation (UFR). In large models, FER may be degrading core model capacities like generalization, creativity, and (continual) learning. Therefore, understanding and mitigating FER could be critical to the future of representation learning.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories.
