The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: When Data Falls Short: Grokking Below the Critical Threshold
papers.research_question: Can knowledge distillation from a grokked model induce and accelerate grokking on a different data distribution, and can grokking occur when training data falls below the critical threshold?
papers.core_contribution: Knowledge Distillation (KD) from a grokked model can induce and accelerate grokking on a different data distribution, even when the available data is below the critical threshold, and does not require weight decay or decreasing weight norms.
papers.conclusion: KD enables grokking below the critical data threshold and across varying distributions, offering a practical solution for efficient training under data scarcity and distribution shift.
papers.key_findings:
KD from a grokked teacher model enables a student model to grok on a different distribution, even when the student's training data is below the critical size.
Grokking can occur without weight decay and with increasing weight norms, challenging prior theories that link grokking to weight norm reduction.
In joint training on two distributions, standard supervised training fails when either distribution has insufficient data, but KD from grokked models enables generalization.
In a continual pretraining setup, KD mitigates catastrophic forgetting when a model transitions from one distribution to another.
KD provides a stronger learning signal than ground-truth labels in low-data regimes, enabling grokking where standard training fails.
future_direction: Extend these insights to more complex tasks.
Deepen our understanding of grokking’s mechanisms.
Explore broader uses of pre-grokked models that generalize reliably and adapt efficiently to dynamic real-world data.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of grokking, where models exhibit delayed generalization following overfitting on training data. We focus on data-scarce regimes where the number of training samples falls below the critical threshold, making grokking unobservable, and on practical scenarios involving distribution shift. We first show that Knowledge Distillation (KD) from a model that has already grokked on a distribution (p1) can induce and accelerate grokking on a different distribution (p2), even when the available data lies below the critical threshold. This highlights the value of KD for deployed models that must adapt to new distributions under limited data. We then study training on the joint distribution (p1, p2) and demonstrate that while standard supervised training fails when either distribution has insufficient data, distilling from models grokked on the individual distributions enables generalization. Finally, we examine a continual pretraining setup, where a grokked model transitions from p1 to p2, and find that KD both accelerates generalization and mitigates catastrophic forgetting, achieving strong performance even with only 10% of the data. Together, our results provide new insights into the mechanics of grokking under knowledge transfer and underscore the central role of KD in enabling generalization in low-data and evolving distribution settings.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers.research_question: Why do heuristics such as cosine annealing (SGDR), learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation improve the convergence and performance of deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to empirically investigate the reasons behind the success of deep learning heuristics like cosine annealing, learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation.
papers.conclusion: The empirical analysis using mode connectivity and CCA sheds light on the heuristics of cosine annealing, warmup, and distillation, suggesting that common explanations are oversimplified and opening new questions for deeper exploration.
papers.key_findings:
The reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing (e.g., escaping local minima) are not evidenced in practice; iterates move over barriers after restarts but this is an oversimplification.
The effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers (e.g., fully-connected stack) from creating training instability; freezing these layers achieves similar outcomes.
In knowledge distillation, the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers of the student network.
Mode connectivity is a robust framework for connecting optima obtained from vastly different training schemes (e.g., different optimizers, batch sizes, regularization).
For SGDR, the path found by mode connectivity corresponds to lower training loss but higher validation loss than the iterates, suggesting a generalization gap.
papers.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers.title: Editing Large Language Models: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently edit large language models to correct errors or update knowledge without negatively impacting performance on other inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey and empirical analysis of model editing methods for large language models, and introduces a new benchmark for evaluating editing techniques.
papers.conclusion: There is much room for improvement in model editing, especially in terms of portability, locality, and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
SERAC and ROME show superior performance on basic editing tasks, but SERAC struggles with portability.
Model editing methods often fail to generalize to related content (portability) and can have side effects on locality.
Some methods like MEMIT support batch editing up to 1000 edits but suffer from decreased locality.
Sequential editing is challenging for methods that modify parameters, with performance degrading over multiple edits.
Efficiency varies across methods, with some requiring extensive pre-computation or training time.
papers.limitation:
Due to computational constraints, only models up to 20B parameters were tested, and architectures like Llama were not explored.
The study primarily focuses on factual knowledge editing, not covering aspects like personality, emotions, opinions, or beliefs.
The evaluation mainly considered single edits; multiple-edit scenarios were not thoroughly evaluated.
Editing black-box LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT-4) is not addressed in detail.
future_direction: Multilingual editing represents an essential research direction.
Editing for non-factual aspects such as personality, emotions, and beliefs.
Developing methods to edit black-box LLMs via in-context learning or prompt-based approaches.
papers.abstract: Despite the ability to train capable LLMs, the methodology for maintaining their relevancy and rectifying errors remains elusive. To this end, the past few years have witnessed a surge in techniques for editing LLMs, the objective of which is to alter the behavior of LLMs efficiently within a specific domain without negatively impacting performance across other inputs. This paper embarks on a deep exploration of the problems, methods, and opportunities related to model editing for LLMs. In particular, we provide an exhaustive overview of the task definition and challenges associated with model editing, along with an in-depth empirical analysis of the most progressive methods currently at our disposal. We also build a new benchmark dataset to facilitate a more robust evaluation and pinpoint enduring issues intrinsic to existing techniques. Our objective is to provide valuable insights into the effectiveness and feasibility of each editing technique, thereby assisting the community in making informed decisions on the selection of the most appropriate method for a specific task or context.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: Who Does What in Deep Learning? Multidimensional Game-Theoretic Attribution of Function of Neural Units
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the contributions of individual neural units (e.g., neurons, experts, filters) to the high-dimensional outputs of deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multiperturbation Shapley-value Analysis (MSA), a model-agnostic, game-theoretic framework that quantifies the causal contributions of individual neural units to scalar or high-dimensional model outputs via systematic perturbation.
papers.conclusion: MSA provides a powerful, general-purpose framework for interpreting, editing, and compressing deep neural networks by quantifying the causal contributions of neural units across diverse architectures and output modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Regularization (L1/L2) concentrates computation into a few critical 'hub' neurons, while unregularized networks distribute function more evenly and show low correlation between neuron weight magnitude and importance.
In the Mixtral 8x7B LLM, different layers specialize in different task domains (e.g., middle layers for arithmetic, first/last layers for factual knowledge), and a single expert (expert 3 in layer 0) is critically important across all domains.
The model contains redundant experts; removing low-contributing experts can sometimes improve performance, while removing high-contributing experts causes severe accuracy drops.
In a DCGAN, an inverted feature hierarchy exists: early transposed convolutional layers contribute to high-level facial features, while later layers contribute to low-level features like edges and colors, contrasting with classification CNNs.
MSA can be used to cluster filters responsible for specific image features (e.g., hair color, teeth) and lesioning these clusters leads to targeted, interpretable changes in the generated images, demonstrating the method's utility for network editing.
papers.limitation:
MSA can be computationally expensive for large models (e.g., taking nearly nine days to run on Mixtral 8x7B on a single A100 GPU).
MSA identifies what each unit contributes but does not elucidate how it performs its function (e.g., the underlying parameters or mechanisms enabling an expert's specialization).
future_direction: Integrating permutation sampling strategies to accelerate the computation of Shapley values.
Extending MSA to analyze interactions between neuron pairs and to multiple dimensions, similar to the approach with Shapley Modes.
papers.abstract: Neural networks now generate text, images, and speech with billions of parameters, producing a need to know how each neural unit contributes to these high-dimensional outputs. Existing explainable-AI methods, such as SHAP, attribute importance to inputs, but cannot quantify the contributions of neural units across thousands of output pixels, tokens, or logits. Here we close that gap with Multiperturbation Shapley-value Analysis (MSA), a model-agnostic game-theoretic framework. By systematically lesioning combinations of units, MSA yields Shapley Modes, unit-wise contribution maps that share the exact dimensionality of the model's output. We apply MSA across scales, from multi-layer perceptrons to the 56-billion-parameter Mixtral-8x7B and Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). The approach demonstrates how regularisation concentrates computation in a few hubs, exposes language-specific experts inside the LLM, and reveals an inverted pixel-generation hierarchy in GANs. Together, these results showcase MSA as a powerful approach for interpreting, editing, and compressing deep neural networks.

papers.title: The Neural Race Reduction: Dynamics of Abstraction in Gated Networks
papers.research_question: How does network architecture (specifically pathways of information flow) affect learning dynamics, representation learning, and generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Gated Deep Linear Network framework and shows that learning dynamics exhibit a neural race bias towards shared representations, enabling systematic generalization and multi-task transfer.
papers.conclusion: The GDLN framework reveals how architecture controls information flow and learning dynamics, leading to a bias towards shared representations that enables systematic generalization and multi-task learning.
papers.key_findings:
The GDLN framework allows exact reduction of learning dynamics to singular value dynamics.
Learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race, with faster learning for pathways that share more structure.
There is an implicit bias towards shared representations, which facilitates zero-shot generalization to untrained input-output pathways.
The dynamics from small random weights converge to the maximally shared solution, as validated on naturalistic datasets.
The degree of sharing required for generalization depends on the fraction of trained pathways, with around 40% sufficient for strong generalization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not provide a mechanism to select the gating structure; it is assumed to be given.
The theoretical analysis assumes diagonalizable dataset statistics and linear networks with gating, though validation is done with relaxed assumptions.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for inferring the optimal architecture and gating for a given setup.
papers.abstract: Our theoretical understanding of deep learning has not kept pace with its empirical success. While network architecture is known to be critical, we do not yet understand its effect on learned representations and network behavior, or how this architecture should reflect task structure.In this work, we begin to address this gap by introducing the Gated Deep Linear Network framework that schematizes how pathways of information flow impact learning dynamics within an architecture. Crucially, because of the gating, these networks can compute nonlinear functions of their input. We derive an exact reduction and, for certain cases, exact solutions to the dynamics of learning. Our analysis demonstrates that the learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race with an implicit bias towards shared representations, which then govern the model's ability to systematically generalize, multi-task, and transfer. We validate our key insights on naturalistic datasets and with relaxed assumptions. Taken together, our work gives rise to general hypotheses relating neural architecture to learning and provides a mathematical approach towards understanding the design of more complex architectures and the role of modularity and compositionality in solving real-world problems. The code and results are available at https://www.saxelab.org/gated-dln .

papers.title: On the Principles of Parsimony and Self-Consistency for the Emergence of Intelligence
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental principles that govern the emergence of intelligence, specifically addressing what to learn and how to learn?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two fundamental principles, Parsimony and Self-consistency, and a unifying computational framework called compressive closed-loop transcription for understanding the emergence of intelligence in both artificial and natural systems.
papers.conclusion: The principles of Parsimony and Self-consistency serve as a cornerstone for the emergence of intelligence and provide a unifying framework for understanding deep networks and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
The Principle of Parsimony states that the objective of learning is to identify and represent low-dimensional structures in observations in the most compact and structured way.
The Principle of Self-consistency states that a learned model must be self-consistent, meaning it can regenerate the original data from its internal representation, forming a closed-loop system.
The two principles lead to a compressive closed-loop transcription framework that unifies discriminative and generative models and enables autonomous, efficient, and stable learning.
Maximizing the rate reduction (ΔR) provides a computable objective for achieving parsimonious representations, leading to structures like independent linear subspaces.
The framework can be extended to unsupervised and incremental learning settings, avoiding problems like catastrophic forgetting and mode collapse.
future_direction: Extending the framework to 3D vision and reinforcement learning.
Exploring the universality of the framework for broader perception and decision-making tasks.
Investigating connections to neuroscience, mathematics, and higher-level intelligence.
papers.abstract: Ten years into the revival of deep networks and artificial intelligence, we propose a theoretical framework that sheds light on understanding deep networks within a bigger picture of Intelligence in general. We introduce two fundamental principles, Parsimony and Self-consistency, that address two fundamental questions regarding Intelligence: what to learn and how to learn, respectively. We believe the two principles are the cornerstones for the emergence of Intelligence, artificial or natural. While these two principles have rich classical roots, we argue that they can be stated anew in entirely measurable and computable ways. More specifically, the two principles lead to an effective and efficient computational framework, compressive closed-loop transcription, that unifies and explains the evolution of modern deep networks and many artificial intelligence practices. While we mainly use modeling of visual data as an example, we believe the two principles will unify understanding of broad families of autonomous intelligent systems and provide a framework for understanding the brain.

papers.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.research_question: Do chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations faithfully represent the true reasons for a model's prediction, or can they be systematically unfaithful by being influenced by biasing features not mentioned in the explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can be plausible yet systematically unfaithful; models can be influenced by biasing features (e.g., option order or suggested answers) without mentioning them in their explanations, rationalizing incorrect or biased predictions.
papers.conclusion: CoT explanations can be misleading, increasing trust in LLMs without guaranteeing safety. Building transparent systems requires either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.
papers.key_findings:
Adding biasing features (e.g., 'Answer is Always A' or 'Suggested Answer') heavily influences model CoT predictions on BBH tasks, causing accuracy to drop by up to 36%.
When biasing features point to incorrect answers, models frequently alter their CoT explanations to justify those incorrect bias-consistent predictions, sometimes with sound reasoning.
On the social bias task (BBQ), models give plausible unfaithful explanations that support answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of stereotypes, using weak evidence inconsistently.
papers.limitation:
Manual evaluation of explanations is costly and subjective.
The study is limited to two models (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0) and a subset of tasks.
The biasing features used are simple and may not cover all ways explanations could be unfaithful.
future_direction: Improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts (e.g., training objectives that incentivize faithful explanations).
Abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods for model transparency and explainability.
Extending the evaluation to more models, tasks, and biasing features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve strong performance on many tasks by producing step-by-step reasoning before giving a final output, often referred to as chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT). It is tempting to interpret these CoT explanations as the LLM's process for solving a task. This level of transparency into LLMs' predictions would yield significant safety benefits. However, we find that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. We demonstrate that CoT explanations can be heavily influenced by adding biasing features to model inputs--e.g., by reordering the multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to make the answer always "(A)"--which models systematically fail to mention in their explanations. When we bias models toward incorrect answers, they frequently generate CoT explanations rationalizing those answers. This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard, when testing with GPT-3.5 from OpenAI and Claude 1.0 from Anthropic. On a social-bias task, model explanations justify giving answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of these social biases. Our findings indicate that CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading, which risks increasing our trust in LLMs without guaranteeing their safety. Building more transparent and explainable systems will require either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.

papers.title: Grokking in LLM Pretraining? Monitor Memorization-to-Generalization without Test
papers.research_question: Specifically, we investigate when an LLM memorizes the training data, when its generalization on downstream tasks starts to improve, and what happens if there is a lag between the two.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first empirical evidence of local, asynchronous grokking in LLM pretraining and introduces two novel, low-cost pathway-based metrics (edit distance and consistency) that accurately track generalization without requiring finetuning or external validation sets.
papers.conclusion: This paper provides the first empirical evidence that, in large-scale LLM pretraining, generalization can emerge well after memorization has been achieved. Through an analysis of routing dynamics in a 7B-parameter MoE model, we propose two novel pathway-based metrics that accurately track generalization without requiring finetuning or external validation sets.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking occurs in LLM pretraining but is local and asynchronous for different data groups, unlike the global grokking observed in small models.
The memorization-to-generalization transition is explained by the dynamics of pathways in MoE: pathway similarity between samples increases and consistency across layers increases.
The two pathway metrics (edit distance and consistency) show strong correlation with downstream generalization performance across diverse benchmarks.
A theoretical connection is established between pathway complexity and a generalization bound for a one-layer MoE.
The pathway metrics provide a finetuning and evaluation-free tool to monitor generalization during pretraining with almost zero cost.
future_direction: Future work will extend these pathway-based metrics beyond MoE, by constructing analogous 'virtual pathways' in dense models, moving toward a unified framework for tracking generalization in foundation models.
papers.abstract: This paper presents the first study of grokking in practical LLM pretraining. Specifically, we investigate when an LLM memorizes the training data, when its generalization on downstream tasks starts to improve, and what happens if there is a lag between the two. Unlike existing works studying when a small model generalizes to limited and specified tasks during thousands epochs' training on algorithmic data, we focus on a practical setting for LLMs, i.e., one-epoch pretraining of next-token prediction on a cross-domain, large-scale corpus, and generalization on diverse benchmark tasks covering math/commonsense reasoning, code generation, and domain-specific retrieval. Our study, for the first time, verifies that grokking still emerges in pretraining mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs, though different local data groups may enter their grokking stages asynchronously due to the heterogeneity of their distributions and attributions to others. To find a mechanistic interpretation of this local grokking, we investigate the dynamics of training data's pathways (i.e., expert choices across layers in MoE). Our primary discovery is that the pathways evolve from random, non-smooth across layers, instance-specific to more structured and transferable across samples, despite the converged pretraining loss. This depicts a transition from memorization to generalization. Two novel metrics are developed to quantify these patterns: one computes the pathway similarity between samples, while the other measures the consistency of aggregated experts between subsequent layers for each sample. These training data based metrics induce zero cost but can faithfully track and monitor the generalization of LLMs on downstream tasks, which, in conventional settings, requires costly instruction tuning and benchmark evaluation.

papers.title: Facts as Experts: Adaptable and Interpretable Neural Memory over\n Symbolic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we interface a neural language model with an interpretable symbolic memory to allow updating facts without retraining and improve performance on knowledge-intensive question answering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural language model with an explicit interface to a symbolic knowledge base, allowing the model to be updated by modifying the symbolic memory without retraining, and shows improved performance on factoid QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a method for interfacing a neural language model with an interpretable symbolically bound memory, enabling updates without retraining and demonstrating effectiveness on factoid QA.
papers.key_findings:
FaE outperforms baseline models (FOFE, EmQL, EaE) on FreebaseQA and WebQuestionsSP, especially when the KB is complete.
FaE can answer some questions without fine-tuning (zero-shot) and outperforms EaE in this setting.
When facts are filtered out during pretraining and fine-tuning, FaE can recover performance by injecting new facts at inference time, while EaE cannot.
FaE can update stale memories by overwriting facts, but performance drops when new facts contradict pretraining data, indicating a challenge in mixing contextual and knowledge representations.
papers.limitation:
When updating stale memories, the model's performance drops because the new facts contradict the pretraining data, making mixing contextual and knowledge representations difficult.
The problem of deleting knowledge is not addressed and is left for future work.
future_direction: Addressing the inconsistency issue when updating facts that contradict pretraining data.
Investigating the problem of deleting knowledge from the model.
papers.abstract:
Massive language models are the core of modern NLP modeling and have been
shown to encode impressive amounts of commonsense and factual information.
However, that knowledge exists only within the latent parameters of the model,
inaccessible to inspection and interpretation, and even worse, factual
information memorized from the training corpora is likely to become stale as
the world changes. Knowledge stored as parameters will also inevitably exhibit
all of the biases inherent in the source materials. To address these problems,
we develop a neural language model that includes an explicit interface between
symbolically interpretable factual information and subsymbolic neural
knowledge. We show that this model dramatically improves performance on two
knowledge-intensive question-answering tasks. More interestingly, the model can
be updated without re-training by manipulating its symbolic representations. In
particular this model allows us to add new facts and overwrite existing ones in
ways that are not possible for earlier models.

papers.title: KQA Pro: A Dataset with Explicit Compositional Programs for Complex Question Answering over Knowledge Base
papers.research_question: How to create a dataset for complex question answering over knowledge bases that addresses the shortcomings of existing benchmarks by providing explicit reasoning processes and diverse, large-scale questions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KQA Pro, a large-scale dataset for complex KBQA with explicit compositional programs (KoPL) and SPARQL queries, serving as a benchmark and diagnostic tool for evaluating reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: KQA Pro is a challenging dataset that can drive further research in complex KBQA, and the introduced KoPL provides interpretability benefits for understanding and correcting model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Existing state-of-the-art KBQA models perform significantly worse on KQA Pro compared to existing datasets, indicating its challenging nature.
Models struggle with comparison reasoning due to lack of literal knowledge.
Models perform poorly on questions whose answers are not observed in the training set.
The KoPL parser can learn multiple semantically correct solutions for a question, similar to human learning.
Providing intermediate program supervision (KoPL) improves model performance and interpretability compared to only answer supervision.
future_direction: Using human correction data to incrementally train the KoPL parser and improve performance continuously.
papers.abstract: Shulin Cao, Jiaxin Shi, Liangming Pan, Lunyiu Nie, Yutong Xiang, Lei Hou, Juanzi Li, Bin He, Hanwang Zhang. Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2022.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding Empirical Unlearning with Combinatorial Interpretability
papers.research_question: Do unlearning methods truly remove knowledge of a target concept, or merely inhibit its expression while retaining the underlying information? How easily can supposedly erased knowledge be recovered through various fine-tuning operations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper uses the combinatorial interpretability framework to show that unlearning methods do not fully remove knowledge; residual knowledge persists in model weights and can be recovered even when fine-tuning on unrelated data, with recovery tending to restore the original network encoding.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning methods leave residual knowledge that can be recovered, and recovery tends to reverse the erasure by moving weights back towards their original state.
papers.key_findings:
Supposedly erased knowledge persists in model weights in a way that can be detected with combinatorial interpretability.
This knowledge resurfaces when fine-tuning the erased model, even on non-target data.
Recovery occurs through a tendency to restore the original (pre-erasure) network encoding, as shown by a high parallel fraction in weight updates.
The encoding structure is largely preserved after Gradient Ascent and Task Vector erasure, but is substantially altered by Privacy Preserving Distillation.
Fine-tuning on unrelated data can recover erased concepts, suggesting erasure leaves residual knowledge attached to the edited weight structure.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on simple two-layer neural networks trained on synthetic DNF data, limiting direct applicability to larger, real-world models.
future_direction: Better understanding of when and why fine-tuning on non-target data restores the original encoding.
Assessing the applicability of these findings to larger models used in practice.
papers.abstract: While many recent methods aim to unlearn or remove knowledge from pretrained models, seemingly erased knowledge often persists and can be recovered in various ways. Because large foundation models are far from interpretable, understanding whether and how such knowledge persists remains a significant challenge. To address this, we turn to the recently developed framework of combinatorial interpretability. This framework, designed for two-layer neural networks, enables direct inspection of the knowledge encoded in the model weights. We reproduce baseline unlearning methods within the combinatorial interpretability setting and examine their behavior along two dimensions: (i) whether they truly remove knowledge of a target concept (the concept we wish to remove) or merely inhibit its expression while retaining the underlying information, and (ii) how easily the supposedly erased knowledge can be recovered through various fine-tuning operations. Our results shed light within a fully interpretable setting on how knowledge can persist despite unlearning and when it might resurface.

papers.title: Entities as Experts: Sparse Memory Access with Entity Supervision
papers.research_question: How can we develop neural sequence models that capture knowledge about real-world entities by learning entity representations directly from text, enabling sparse memory access?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Entities as Experts (EAE), a transformer-based model that learns entity representations directly from text and accesses them sparsely via an entity memory layer, demonstrating improved performance on knowledge probing and question answering tasks compared to larger models.
papers.conclusion: EAE effectively captures declarative knowledge in entity representations and outperforms larger models on knowledge-intensive tasks, but it cannot handle unseen entities and future work should explore representations for rare entities and integration with knowledge bases.
papers.key_findings:
EAE outperforms larger models like BERT-large and T5-3B on TriviaQA and LAMA knowledge probes.
Supervision via entity linking is crucial for the entity memory layer's performance; unsupervised memory access performs worse.
EAE's learned entity representations are more effective than pre-trained embeddings from KNOWBERT and ERNIE on knowledge probing tasks.
Sparse access (retrieving top-k entity memories) works effectively with little performance drop, enabling efficient inference.
Correct identification and linking of entity mentions in questions is essential for EAE's question answering performance.
papers.limitation:
Cannot handle unseen entities due to fixed entity vocabulary.
Poor performance on non-entity concepts such as dates and common nouns.
future_direction: Explore representations for rare or unseen entities.
Develop less memory-intensive ways to learn and integrate entity representations.
Integrate information from external knowledge bases to improve entity representations.
papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of capturing declarative knowledge about entities in the learned parameters of a language model. We introduce a new model-Entities as Experts (EAE)that can access distinct memories of the entities mentioned in a piece of text. Unlike previous efforts to integrate entity knowledge into sequence models, EAE's entity representations are learned directly from text. We show that EAE's learned representations capture sufficient knowledge to answer TriviaQA questions such as "Which Dr. Who villain has been played by Roger Delgado, Anthony Ainley, Eric Roberts?", outperforming an encodergenerator Transformer model with 10 the parameters. According to the LAMA knowledge probes, EAE contains more factual knowledge than a similarly sized BERT, as well as previous approaches that integrate external sources of entity knowledge. Because EAE associates parameters with specific entities, it only needs to access a fraction of its parameters at inference time, and we show that the correct identification and representation of entities is essential to EAE's performance.

papers.title: Half-Space Feature Learning in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn features? The paper investigates whether neural networks learn simple half-space features and how gradient descent allocates resources (paths) to different regions of the input space.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), a model that learns simple half-space features, and shows that feature learning in neural networks involves gradient descent allocating more paths to easier regions of the input space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn simple half-space features, and that gradient descent allocates more resources to easier regions, which can be visualized in DLGNs, providing enhanced interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DLGNs can perform comparably to ReLU networks on datasets like CIFAR-10 while being more interpretable.
Feature learning in neural networks involves changes in the active path regions, which can be tracked via the overlap kernel.
Gradient descent tends to allocate more paths (resources) to regions of the input space where the target function is simpler (lower frequency).
The empirical NTK changes during training to become better suited to the task, and this change is driven by the evolution of active path regions.
In DLGNs, neurons in later layers tend to specialize to simpler regions (e.g., half-spaces) that cover low-frequency parts of the target function.
papers.limitation: Analysis of ReLU networks is complicated due to their complex path active regions, so the study uses DLGNs as a surrogate.
future_direction: Investigating defects of gradient descent in resource allocation and developing architecture-aware optimization algorithms.
Further study of the phenomenon of neurons focusing on easy regions.
papers.abstract: There currently exist two extreme viewpoints for neural network feature learning -- (i) Neural networks simply implement a kernel method (a la NTK) and hence no features are learned (ii) Neural networks can represent (and hence learn) intricate hierarchical features suitable for the data. We argue in this paper neither interpretation is likely to be correct based on a novel viewpoint. Neural networks can be viewed as a mixture of experts, where each expert corresponds to a (number of layers length) path through a sequence of hidden units. We use this alternate interpretation to motivate a model, called the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), which sits midway between deep linear networks and ReLU networks. Unlike deep linear networks, the DLGN is capable of learning non-linear features (which are then linearly combined), and unlike ReLU networks these features are ultimately simple -- each feature is effectively an indicator function for a region compactly described as an intersection of (number of layers) half-spaces in the input space. This viewpoint allows for a comprehensive global visualization of features, unlike the local visualizations for neurons based on saliency/activation/gradient maps. Feature learning in DLGNs is shown to happen and the mechanism with which this happens is through learning half-spaces in the input space that contain smooth regions of the target function. Due to the structure of DLGNs, the neurons in later layers are fundamentally the same as those in earlier layers -- they all represent a half-space -- however, the dynamics of gradient descent impart a distinct clustering to the later layer neurons. We hypothesize that ReLU networks also have similar feature learning behaviour.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Two-phase perspective on deep learning dynamics
papers.research_question: Does learning in deep neural networks proceed in two distinct phases (curve-fitting followed by compression), and are the phenomena of grokking, double descent, and the information bottleneck linked by this common temporal structure?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that deep learning involves two phases (curve-fitting then compression) and shows that grokking, double descent, and the information bottleneck share a common temporal structure aligned with these phases.
papers.conclusion: Learning in deep neural networks proceeds in two phases: a rapid curve-fitting phase and a slower compression phase essential for generalization, with mutual information I(T;X) acting as a process measure for the latter.
papers.key_findings:
The time scales marking the transition from curve-fitting to compression in grokking, double descent, and the information bottleneck are empirically aligned.
Mutual information between hidden layers and input data (I(T;X)) serves as a natural progress measure for the compression phase, decreasing as the network generalizes.
The compression phase is characterized by a reduction in the number of linear regions (circuits) and in mutual information I(T;X), reflecting a form of 'forgetting' of irrelevant input details.
The second (compression) phase is not actively optimized by standard training algorithms and may be unnecessarily prolonged.
The compression phase resembles coarse-graining in the renormalization group, suggesting a principled form of forgetting critical for generalization.
future_direction: Developing tailored training algorithms that deliberately promote compression to accelerate the path to generalization.
Further developing the circuit-based perspective and applying it to detailed studies of the second phase dynamics.
papers.abstract: We propose that learning in deep neural networks proceeds in two phases: a rapid curve-fitting phase followed by a slower compression or coarse-graining phase. This view is supported by the shared temporal structure of three phenomena-grokking, double descent, and the information bottleneck-all of which exhibit a delayed onset of generalization well after training error reaches zero. We empirically show that the associated timescales align in two rather different settings. Mutual information between hidden layers and input data emerges as a natural progress measure, complementing circuit-based metrics such as local complexity and the linear mapping number. We argue that the second phase is not actively optimized by standard training algorithms and may be unnecessarily prolonged. Drawing on an analogy with the renormalization group, we suggest that this compression phase reflects a principled form of forgetting, critical for generalization.

papers.title: Measuring Information Transfer in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How to measure the generalizable information in a neural network model? The paper proposes a measure called Information Transfer (LIT) based on prequential coding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Information Transfer (LIT), a measure based on prequential coding, to estimate the generalizable information in a neural network model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Information Transfer (LIT) is a practical measure of generalizable information in neural networks and can serve as a useful tool for analyzing deep learning problems from an information perspective.
papers.key_findings:
LIT is consistently correlated with generalizable information and can be used as a measure of patterns or knowledge in a model or dataset.
LIT can dissect the information content of a dataset, as shown in the CIFAR-10 subtasks analysis.
In transfer learning, the Information Advantage (LIA) derived from LIT measures the quality of pre-trained representation models.
In continual learning, LIT measures the information preserved about past tasks, revealing that catastrophic forgetting is less severe in terms of information loss than performance metrics suggest.
LIT provides an information perspective that helps discover new insights into neural network learning, such as the dynamics of information transfer and forgetting.
papers.limitation: The quality of the approximation is hard to guarantee theoretically due to lack of analysis on convergence properties of prequential coding.
future_direction: Develop learning algorithms to maximize generalizable model knowledge.
papers.abstract: Quantifying the information content in a neural network model is essentially estimating the model's Kolmogorov complexity. Recent success of prequential coding on neural networks points to a promising path of deriving an efficient description length of a model. We propose a practical measure of the generalizable information in a neural network model based on prequential coding, which we term Information Transfer ($L_{IT}$). Theoretically, $L_{IT}$ is an estimation of the generalizable part of a model's information content. In experiments, we show that $L_{IT}$ is consistently correlated with generalizable information and can be used as a measure of patterns or "knowledge" in a model or a dataset. Consequently, $L_{IT}$ can serve as a useful analysis tool in deep learning. In this paper, we apply $L_{IT}$ to compare and dissect information in datasets, evaluate representation models in transfer learning, and analyze catastrophic forgetting and continual learning algorithms. $L_{IT}$ provides an information perspective which helps us discover new insights into neural network learning.

papers.title: Unveiling and Consulting Core Experts in Retrieval-Augmented MoE-based LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms within MoE-based LLMs that contribute to the effectiveness of RAG systems, and how can expert activations be used to improve RAG?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies core experts in MoE-based LLMs that are responsible for RAG-related behaviors and proposes strategies to enhance RAG efficiency and effectiveness by leveraging expert activations.
papers.conclusion: Experimental results across various datasets and MoE-based LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving RAG.
papers.key_findings:
Cognizant experts indicate the sufficiency of the model's internal knowledge.
Quality experts assess the quality of retrieved documents.
In-context experts enhance the model's ability to utilize contextual information.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly improved the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. While existing research seeks to enhance RAG performance by retrieving higher-quality documents or designing RAG-specific LLMs, the internal mechanisms within LLMs that contribute to the effectiveness of RAG systems remain underexplored. In this paper, we aim to investigate these internal mechanisms within the popular Mixture-of-Expert (MoE)-based LLMs and demonstrate how to improve RAG by examining expert activations in these LLMs. Our controlled experiments reveal that several core groups of experts are primarily responsible for RAG-related behaviors. The activation of these core experts can signify the model's inclination towards external/internal knowledge and adjust its behavior. For instance, we identify core experts that can (1) indicate the sufficiency of the model's internal knowledge, (2) assess the quality of retrieved documents, and (3) enhance the model's ability to utilize context. Based on these findings, we propose several strategies to enhance RAG's efficiency and effectiveness through expert activation. Experimental results across various datasets and MoE-based LLMs show the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Collective variables of neural networks: empirical time evolution and scaling laws
papers.research_question: How can the entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) be used to understand learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel as collective variables to analyze neural network training dynamics, identifying two learning regimes (information compression and structure formation) and showing that structure formation characterizes the deep learning regime.
papers.conclusion: Entropy and trace of the NTK provide a universal framework for understanding neural network learning dynamics and scaling, with structure formation identified as a hallmark of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy of the NTK reveals two learning regimes: information compression (entropy decreases) where gradient vectors align, and structure formation (entropy increases) where the network separates data to create richer representations.
Small networks tend to remain in the compression regime with limited performance, while large networks transition to structure formation, which is associated with improved performance and defines a deep learning regime.
The trace of the NTK, representing an effective learning rate, increases during training, indicating growing network sensitivity to new data and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks or benefits for continual learning.
The dynamics observed via entropy and trace are universal across diverse architectures including transformers, GNNs, CNNs, and reinforcement learning agents.
Architecture scaling (width and depth) influences the entropy and trace, with deeper networks showing reduced entropy at initialization but capable of achieving higher entropy after training when sufficiently wide.
future_direction: Explore how scaling behavior for different activation functions can be used for targeted architecture selection.
Investigate the trace property to reduce model sensitivity and improve continual learning strategies.
Explore avenues for improved stability by reducing trace late in training.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel means for understanding learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks. We show that certain measures on the spectrum of the empirical neural tangent kernel, specifically entropy and trace, yield insight into the representations learned by a neural network and how these can be improved through architecture scaling. These results are demonstrated first on test cases before being shown on more complex networks, including transformers, auto-encoders, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning studies. In testing on a wide range of architectures, we highlight the universal nature of training dynamics and further discuss how it can be used to understand the mechanisms behind learning in neural networks. We identify two such dominant mechanisms present throughout machine learning training. The first, information compression, is seen through a reduction in the entropy of the NTK spectrum during training, and occurs predominantly in small neural networks. The second, coined structure formation, is seen through an increasing entropy and thus, the creation of structure in the neural network representations beyond the prior established by the network at initialization. Due to the ubiquity of the latter in deep neural network architectures and its flexibility in the creation of feature-rich representations, we argue that this form of evolution of the network's entropy be considered the onset of a deep learning regime.

papers.title: Concept Distillation: Leveraging Human-Centered Explanations for Model Improvement
papers.research_question: If CAVs can identify and quantify sensitivity to concepts, can they also be used to improve the model? Can we learn less biased and more human-centered models?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) from post-hoc analysis to ante-hoc model improvement via a concept loss and concept distillation using a teacher model, enabling model debiasing and prior knowledge induction.
papers.conclusion: Concept distillation and concept loss provide a framework for improving model interpretability, reducing biases, and inducing prior knowledge by leveraging human-centered explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Concept-sensitive training with a concept loss can debias models on synthetic (ColorMNIST, DecoyMNIST, TextureMNIST) and real-world (BFFHQ) datasets.
Using a large pre-trained teacher model (DINO) for concept distillation improves concept learning and debiasing performance compared to using the student model alone.
Extending CAV sensitivity calculation to intermediate layers via class prototypes enhances the method's effectiveness.
The method can induce human-centered concepts as priors in non-classification tasks, demonstrated on Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID).
The approach is zero-shot and does not require architectural changes or direct concept supervision.
papers.abstract: Humans use abstract concepts for understanding instead of hard features. Recent interpretability research has focused on human-centered concept explanations of neural networks. Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) estimate a model's sensitivity and possible biases to a given concept. In this paper, we extend CAVs from post-hoc analysis to ante-hoc training in order to reduce model bias through fine-tuning using an additional Concept Loss. Concepts were defined on the final layer of the network in the past. We generalize it to intermediate layers using class prototypes. This facilitates class learning in the last convolution layer, which is known to be most informative. We also introduce Concept Distillation to create richer concepts using a pre-trained knowledgeable model as the teacher. Our method can sensitize or desensitize a model towards concepts. We show applications of concept-sensitive training to debias several classification problems. We also use concepts to induce prior knowledge into IID, a reconstruction problem. Concept-sensitive training can improve model interpretability, reduce biases, and induce prior knowledge. Please visit https://avani17101.github.io/Concept-Distilllation/ for code and more details.

papers.title: Interpreting Graph Neural Networks for NLP With Differentiable Edge\n Masking
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Graph Neural Networks for NLP by identifying which edges in the input graph contribute to predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GRAPH MASK, a post-hoc interpretation method for GNNs that learns to mask superfluous edges in a differentiable and amortized way, providing faithful attributions of edge importance.
papers.conclusion: GRAPH MASK is a faithful, scalable post-hoc interpretation method for GNNs that can identify how edges and paths influence predictions, as demonstrated on QA and SRL tasks.
papers.key_findings:
On a synthetic task, amortized GRAPH MASK accurately identifies important edges (F1=99.4), while baselines like erasure search and GNNExplainer suffer from hindsight bias and low recall.
On QA, only 27% of edges are retained, with the majority in the bottom layer, and the model relies on COREF edges only when string match edges are not available.
On SRL, the scalar gates in the original model act as scaling rather than filtering, and thus are not suitable for interpretation.
For SRL, the GNN relies on dependency paths, especially for long-distance arguments, and the importance of paths varies between nominal and verbal predicates.
GRAPH MASK is stable across random seeds, with high Fleiss' Kappa agreement (0.65 for QA, 0.79 and 0.74 for SRL models).
future_direction: Applying GRAPH MASK to other domains beyond NLP.
papers.abstract:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a popular approach to integrating
structural inductive biases into NLP models. However, there has been little
work on interpreting them, and specifically on understanding which parts of the
graphs (e.g. syntactic trees or co-reference structures) contribute to a
prediction. In this work, we introduce a post-hoc method for interpreting the
predictions of GNNs which identifies unnecessary edges. Given a trained GNN
model, we learn a simple classifier that, for every edge in every layer,
predicts if that edge can be dropped. We demonstrate that such a classifier can
be trained in a fully differentiable fashion, employing stochastic gates and
encouraging sparsity through the expected $L_0$ norm. We use our technique as
an attribution method to analyze GNN models for two tasks -- question answering
and semantic role labeling -- providing insights into the information flow in
these models. We show that we can drop a large proportion of edges without
deteriorating the performance of the model, while we can analyse the remaining
edges for interpreting model predictions.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Self-Assembling Modular Networks for Interpretable Multi-Hop Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we perform interpretable multi-hop reasoning in question answering by dynamically assembling neural modules based on the question?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents an interpretable, controller-based self-assembling modular network for multi-hop reasoning, with novel modules (Find, Relocate, Compare, NoOp) designed for language reasoning, achieving improved performance and demonstrating interpretable compositional reasoning behavior.
papers.conclusion: The proposed self-assembling neural modular network for multi-hop QA outperforms baselines and, due to its interpretable nature, is shown to learn and perform compositional reasoning by dynamically assembling modules based on the question.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed modular network significantly outperforms both a single-hop bi-attention baseline and the original convolution-based NMN on the HotpotQA dataset.
The controller learns to decompose multi-hop questions into sub-questions and predicts module layouts that match expert-designed layouts with high accuracy.
The model demonstrates robust compositional reasoning, as shown by strong performance on an adversarial evaluation that eliminates single-hop shortcuts.
Intermediate modules can successfully infer bridge entities that connect distantly located supporting facts.
Ablation studies show that each novel module (Relocate, Compare, NoOp) contributes to the model's overall performance on different question types.
papers.abstract: Yichen Jiang, Mohit Bansal. Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP). 2019.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: ExpertWeaver: Unlocking the Inherent MoE in Dense LLMs with GLU Activation Patterns
papers.research_question: How can pretrained dense language models be effectively converted into sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures without breaking their intrinsic activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExpertWeaver, a training-free framework that converts dense LLMs into MoE architectures by leveraging the inherent activation patterns of Gated Linear Unit (GLU) neurons to partition them into shared and routed experts.
papers.conclusion: ExpertWeaver is an effective, training-free method for converting dense models into high-performance MoEs by leveraging intrinsic GLU activation patterns, outperforming existing approaches in both inference efficiency and model downcycling.
papers.key_findings:
GLU activation patterns in dense LLMs reveal an inherent MoE structure composed of universally active neurons and specialized, task-specific neurons.
ExpertWeaver significantly outperforms existing training-free structural pruning and MoE downcycling methods across multiple benchmarks.
Layer-specific expert allocation, based on the Coefficient of Variation (CV) of neuron activations, is crucial for optimal MoE construction.
The method provides a superior initialization for sparse MoEs, enabling high performance with minimal continued pretraining compared to training from scratch or upcycling.
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) effectively scales model capacity while preserving computational efficiency through sparse expert activation. However, training high-quality MoEs from scratch is prohibitively expensive. A promising alternative is to convert pretrained dense models into sparse MoEs. Existing dense-to-MoE methods fall into two categories: \textbf{dynamic structural pruning} that converts dense models into MoE architectures with moderate sparsity to balance performance and inference efficiency, and \textbf{downcycling} approaches that use pretrained dense models to initialize highly sparse MoE architectures. However, existing methods break the intrinsic activation patterns within dense models, leading to suboptimal expert construction. In this work, we argue that the Gated Linear Unit (GLU) mechanism provides a natural blueprint for dense-to-MoE conversion. We show that the fine-grained neural-wise activation patterns of GLU reveal a coarse-grained structure, uncovering an inherent MoE architecture composed of consistently activated universal neurons and dynamically activated specialized neurons. Leveraging this discovery, we introduce ExpertWeaver, a training-free framework that partitions neurons according to their activation patterns and constructs shared experts and specialized routed experts with layer-adaptive configurations. Our experiments demonstrate that ExpertWeaver significantly outperforms existing methods, both as a training-free dynamic structural pruning technique and as a downcycling strategy for superior MoE initialization.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
